We evaluate the decay length of $B^0_s$ mesons turning into $K^+K^-$ pairs,
utilizing a dataset spanning 11.6 inverse nanoseconds in proper decay time
and sourced from $J/\psi j\jet$ events. Our methodology involves studying
the $B^0_s$ meson's invariant mass near the $J/\psi$ resonance, either alone
or in conjunction with an associated $J/\psi$. Effectively decay widths are
calculated as follows: $\Gamma_{eff}^{(0)} = 0.460 \pm 0.010 \, \text{fs}$,
$\Gamma_{eff}^{(2)} = 0.469 \pm 0.011 \, \text{fs}$, and their average
$\Gamma_{eff}^{(ave)} = 0.466 \pm 0.009 \, \text{fs}$ aligns well with the
established $\Gamma_{bs}$ value of $0.461 \, \text{fs}^{-1}$ derived from
global fits of $B^0_s$ oscillation and decay width parameters.

This study looks at a continuous stochastic control problem where the underlying asset price follows a log-normal distribution and can transition between states. The examination includes a specific scenario involving a Poisson process and a broader context with a generic Sch\"{a}fer-type generator. The investigation demonstrates the existence and uniqueness of the solution to this problem, provides a method for solving it, and demonstrates the convergence of the solution to the discretized model. The continuous random logarithmic spot rate model is also demonstrated to be a convergent scheme for a continuous stochastic control problem with a Sch\"{a}fer-type generator. The proposed model has the potential to be utilized for pricing real-world assets, such as real options within a hydroelectric dam project, by utilizing the discrete-time lattice method. The theoretical findings are supplemented with a numerical example.

Our analysis of high-energy primary particles above 4 EeV in energy revealed a significant anisotropy in their arrival directions, found in nearly 33% of closely related particle groups exhibiting an excess of arrivals within 50 degrees of Centaurus A. We assessed the statistical significance of this trend considering various systematic errors and laboratory inaccuracies. Energy reconstruction was modified by incorporating calibration constants for individual detector components. An independent analysis was also conducted at 8 EeV, which yielded similar results. These outcomes are also discussed in relation to observations from other experiments such as the Telescope Array.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) enabled the study of charged particle properties and nuclear alteration factors in p+Pb collisions. Researchers analyzed nine rapidity intervals and two transverse momentum ranges to determine particle distributions and nuclear alteration factors. These were calculated for nine distinct y ranges and two tT ranges, using data from ATLAS for 5.02 TeV p+Pb and 2012 TeV pb collisions. The results were compared to pp collisions at 2012 TeV by dividing particle yields in p+Pb collisions by the yield in pb collisions. Additionally, theoretical models including PYTHIA 6.4, SGET and a p+Pb model were evaluated against experimental data. The analysis revealed an alteration of charged particle distributions and alteration factors due to nuclear effects.

The study focuses on time-evolution processes within noncommutative probability that preserve a star operation, utilizing techniques from both classical and noncommutative dynamics. Various models are analyzed, including those related to the su(2) and so(3) Lie algebras. A general framework for both dissipative and conservative dynamical processes has also been proposed.

In our work, we address a federated learning challenge specific to medical imaging. The issue arises when multiple hospitals have historical X-ray images and want to train a model to count tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes within those images. Each hospital's data is private, and they are unaware of the presence or sizes of tumors in their patients' images. To tackle this challenge, we developed a federated training approach using agnostic meta-learning. This allows them to train a model in a few-shot setting without direct access to the imaging data or tumor information. Interestingly, our proposed method can also be applied to conventional multi-client training by treating each hospital as a client, and it outperforms conventional techniques in this scenario as well. We conducted multiple multi-client experiments to validate the effectiveness of the approach and demonstrated improved performance compared to conventional federated learning and local training methods.

Underwater communications are critical for subsea exploration and the safety of offshore drilling operations. High-speed decision feedback equalizers (DFEs) are a vital component of these systems. However, pressure sensors used in these systems generate high-pressure fluctuations known as microbursts that can distort equalization decisions and lead to bursts of errors. To mitigate this issue, a novel equalization strategy is proposed in which the weights of the DFE are dynamically adjusted, allowing for the separation of signal bursts and pressure fluctuations. To test this approach, an end-to-end communication system was designed and tested in a high-pressure underwater environment, demonstrating the efficacy of adaptive DFE in successfully mitigating microbursts and maintaining data integrity. Furthermore, this technique can be applied to a variety of underwater communication scenarios and pressure conditions.

Deep Learning techniques have been adapted for Time Series Data, with State-of-the-Art models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) achieving significant success. TCNs employ Temporal Convolutional Layers that expand in channel size, which has been found to be overly complex and inefficient for models trained across multiple time steps. Our TCN-Optimized Network Trimming (PIT) model removes unnecessary parameters from TCNs, enhancing its efficiency without compromising performance. We integrate TCN-Optimized layers into a TCN framework that functions seamlessly with standard training procedures. Notably, PIT's efficiency gains are particularly pronounced when using larger preprocessing vocabularies. Our experiments demonstrate that PIT outperforms established models such as TCNs, Convolutional Neural Networks with Multiple Attraction Fields (MAR-CNNs), and Attention-based Neural Networks (LSTM-TCNs) in both accuracy and efficiency.
The lower central series of a free zinbiel algebra of characteristic not equal to 2 has been found to be strictly decreasing, which implies that all zinbiel algebras are solvable.

Utilizing returbinence theory, we employ the Navier-Stokes equation to determine the average transverse transverse momentum transfer (approximately 0.15 times the average gradient of the spatial gradient of the stress tensor), which is critical for understanding the characteristics of the lead-lead collisions. In the context of unified differential logics, a specific system known as the identity rule addresses the challenge of reversing a differential operation by utilizing the system's pointwise unification property. This paper explores how the identity rule can be derived from more fundamental principles, specifically the basic unification principle, within the framework of Star-autonomous categories with comonoidal laws.

In maintaining accuracy of tabular datasets that evolve over time, ensuring they reflect underlying facts seamlessly is the primary goal. However, achieving this objective becomes complex when datasets contain errors such as missing values and violate dependency rules, limiting existing approaches to datasets without inaccuracies or those containing only simple missing values. To tackle these challenges jointly, we have devised a framework called DARLING, which identifies the cheapest set of actions to revert to a previous state without errors or unmet dependencies. Further, we have designed the DARLING algorithm to pinpoint a localized area of the dataset, revise it to eliminate errors and unmet dependencies, with minimal actions akin to adding, deleting, or shifting values. We have evaluated DARLING's performance through the use of progressively larger synthetic datasets and real-world data, demonstrating its capability to efficiently restore the integrity of tabular datasets.

For modeling time series data with count values, existing methods have limited capability in handling large datasets and varying intensity patterns over time. A new variant of the TVPAR model is introduced to cope with these challenges. TVPAR employs a tensor decomposition technique to efficiently capture complex intensity patterns in time series data. Experimental evaluations using real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate the advantages of TVPAR in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. A key feature of TVPAR is its scalability, allowing it to process large datasets without sacrificing performance. Additionally, an open-source implementation of TVPAR is made available for further use and improvement by the research community.

This paper introduces Neural Description Fields (NDFs), a novel way to represent objects that changes seamlessly as they move through space. NDFs consist of multiple camera views, each capturing the object from a specific angle. What sets NDFs apart is their unique property: as an object moves, its appearance from any given camera viewpoint remains consistently identical. To achieve this, this paper utilizes Selection Equivariance, allowing NDFs to accurately track 3D object motion in the air. Additionally, NDFs can leverage rich, high-dimensional descriptions of static objects available in existing descriptions, such as Shape Functions (SFs), to bring benefits including reliable descriptive power and efficient processing in neural networks. The framework of NDFs can also serve as a subset of Selection Equivariant Object Representations (SEORs). Experimental results demonstrate that our approach uses fewer parameters and performs better in space than comparable methods in terms of object handling tasks.

The concept of the $\mathrm{SiD}$ Magnet has been widely adopted as a design template for the central magnetic component of the ILC detector concept. $\mathrm{SiD}$ stands for "Solenoid in Double Dipole", and its primary feature is a highly sophisticated silicon vertex detector positioned close to the $\mathrm{SiD}$'s central magnetic field. However, implementing this type of advanced silicon detector in a $2$ T double dipole field presents significant technical challenges. Consequently, alternative designs have been explored, such as relocating the silicon detector to an area with a stronger $10$ T solenoid field surrounding the $2$ T $ \mathrm{SiD}$, or adopting entirely new designs. This paper delves into a range of detector designs and provides an in-depth examination of their respective advantages and disadvantages.

We investigated the stellar properties of a dense core in a fragmented globular cluster system, identified as Super-Remnant 2, consisting of individual clusters and a flow of gas called Tonantzintla 2. Using the Near-infrared Integral Field Spectrograph, we conducted a detailed analysis of the clusters' ages, chemical compositions, and stellar velocities in various parts of the remnant. Our data revealed significant variations in metallicity across the region, with a distinct trend toward higher metallicity in the inner areas. Furthermore, we discovered that the stellar velocities in the inner areas match the escape velocity of the Milky Way's bulge, suggesting a potential unbound system. Based on a statistical analysis of the color differences between the individual clusters and a nearby flow of stars called H1821-64, we estimated that Tonantzintla 2 may have been torn apart due to a supernova explosion approximately 3.9 billion years ago.

The proliferation of verification tools in the past decade has laid a robust foundation for the safety and dependability of critical computer systems. However, the intricate nature of mathematical proofs can pose an insurmountable barrier for non-experts in the field. To address this hurdle, research on human-friendly theorem demonstrations has sought to simplify complex proofs by breaking them down into manageable components, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying logic. Although significant progress has been made in this area, there are still areas for improvement, including the need for more transparency and modularity in the proof structure. To advance the field, we have compiled a framework that serves as a guide for the development of human-centric theorem demonstrations, offering a set of criteria to evaluate and enhance the effectiveness of these demonstrations. By leveraging the rich repository of pre-verified theorems in Isabelle's Archive of Formal Proofs, researchers can build upon a solid foundation of trusted knowledge to develop more efficient and comprehensible proofs. To illustrate the value of our framework, we have focused on two challenging topics in linear systems theory, specifically controllability and observability, and showcased how the principles of human-friendly theorem demonstrations can be applied to streamline the logical structure of the proofs by utilizing advanced techniques such as reachability functors.

Building on earlier findings, we expand the connection between group theory and Yang-Lee zero criticality for traditional order parameters across O(N) universality classes. Specifically, we pinpoint the critical behavior for traditional symmetries by identifying the smallest non-trivial irreducible representation within these groups. For parameters with traditional symmetry, we then apply an general method to calculate exponents by using the spins of these representations. Using this method, we obtain calculated values for critical parameters in Yang-Lee zero density for traditional order parameters across various ferromagnets, finding close correlations with established experimental results. Our method is then applied to predict critical behavior for traditional order parameters in Heisenberg and Potts models.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a desired optimal solution lies within a local minimum's basin of attraction. Recent evidence (see refs. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) indicates that, under certain asymptotic conditions, most optimization algorithms become trapped in suboptimal local minima far from the global minimum. Notably, refs. 2 and 6 highlight how the emergence of these numerous pathological local minima can be smoothly and continuously described using the approximate message passing algorithm, an iterative solution. This discovery significantly enhances the comprehension of phase transitions within various optimization models, including those related to the noreplization problem, tensor spin glasses, and community detection. This work introduces a novel, general technique (based on the Sudakov-Fernique lemma) to prove the confinement of optimization algorithms within specific basins of attraction, in addition to providing a new proof of the local convexity of the TAP free energy.

Modern metasurfaces, which are ultra-thin and highly integrated electronic systems built on top of ultra-large scale integrated circuits, present an exciting opportunity for manipulating electromagnetic waves in innovative ways. However, verifying the computational models of these metasurfaces can be a laborious and time-consuming process when employing traditional full-wave electromagnetic solvers due to their data intensity. This examination utilizes three distinct computational methods to efficiently verify the performance of metasurfaces by leveraging simplified calculations over frequency ranges, which can be easily validated through simple measurements. In a practical application, we successfully predicted and experimentally confirmed the characteristics of a metasurface which mimics an inductor at multiple frequencies and an actual chip which integrates this inductive element in an antenna, demonstrating the effectiveness of this efficient verification approach.

The primary objective of this research is to verify the conjecture that a smooth, positively invariant limit cycle arises from the orbital linearization of a vector field with a singularity at the origin in R^n, if and only if the vector field can be transformed into a normalized form with a coefficient representing the cycle equal to 1. Additionally, this condition can be fulfilled even in the absence of normal forms capable of achieving a normalized coefficient equal to 1. The proof of this statement is provided for two integrable vector fields: a family with a focus at the origin and one with a singularity capable of producing a limit cycle, as well as an explicit example of a vector field where the normalized form's coefficient represents the presence or absence of a limit cycle.

This investigation focuses on developing an electronic structure method capable of accurately capturing the full CI electron correlations in molecules. To achieve this, we propose using a slanted neural network to efficiently select an ultra compact molecular orbital basis from a large virtual space. By drastically reducing the dimensionality of the optimization problem, we demonstrate that the network can achieve accurate results even with a minimal optimized basis, matching the high computational costs associated with the full CI references. The efficiency of the approach allows for direct use of full CI references without the need for lower bounds. The method's flexibility is further highlighted by its adaptability to different systems and its potential for real-time applications, particularly when combined with on-the-fly sampling techniques. The concept's computational advantages over traditional methods like configuration interaction with a single reference are explored, while maintaining the high accuracy of electron correlation handling. The potential of using reinforcement learning to train the network in different scenarios, possibly reducing the need for extensive computational resources, is also discussed.

We discovered a massive galaxy group in the centre of a massive galaxy cluster called SDSSJ1250. Considering its position and mass, it should be extremely bright and active, yet it emits very little radiation. Its dark matter profile appears irregular, possibly due to recent galaxy mergers.

Investigating M-dwarf photometry offers an uncomplicated yet highly effective means of monitoring scattering indicators resulting from atmospheric aerosols. While the influence of aerosols on a stellar point source can result in color changes detectable in photometric data, the presence of lunar halos presents a comparable phenomenon. Unlike the diverse aerosol distributions that influence the interstellar medium, the atmospheric aerosol system is governed by a unified distribution. To precisely measure atmospheric aerosols utilizing photometric color measures, a new formalism has been developed which compensates for the inherent bias of these systems. This new approach will primarily depend on the ability to model atmospheric radiative transfer and detect subtle shifts in the position of the stellar spectrum relative to the width of narrow spectral features. The proposed method utilizes the difference in how the stellar spectrum and the surrounding system perceive broad bandwidth filters to determine excess aerosol scattering, or extinction, at those specific wavelengths. To provide a practical reference for this method, its predicted accuracy has been simulated for a stellar spectrum observed through mild atmospheric conditions and mapped to a real cosmic example by utilizing recent measurements of the foreground galactic dust extinction along the D25 quasar's path, which can be independently verified through the quasar's direct spectral analysis.

This paper introduces DeepHMap++, a novel approach for accurately predicting an object's three-dimensional pose based on a single color image. Building on the existing DeepHMap method, we made significant improvements by utilizing a spherical parameterization to represent the object's six degrees of freedom pose and integrating correspondence learning with histogram-based clustering. Specifically, we modified the DeepHMap's histogram-based clustering technique by using a merged spherical projection to cluster corresponding points, which enhanced the method's robustness, particularly in objects with repetitive patterns. These changes led to increased performance, outmatching DeepHMap's mean average error by 0.12 axes and 0.10 overall in our experiment.

Nonlocal integral models have gained significant importance in describing materials with unpredictable failure and enhanced fracture propagation, and their complexity can be reduced to the basic bond-breaking concepts, resulting in a practical and effective description. While the nature of nonlocal interactions in the theoretical framework has no limitations in spatial extent, research indicates that these models can be aligned with the bond-breaking principles by limiting their influence to a finite range. Although the exact limit does not appear to be a critical factor, as long as it exceeds a certain threshold, the bond-oriented nonlocal model successfully represents the fundamental characteristics of materials. Interestingly, this model also enables accurate representation of the complex interaction between fractures and fluids within the context of fluid-mechanics, raising intriguing possibilities for further exploration.

Graphical Lasso is a widely used algorithm for estimating a precision matrix, but there is a lack of flexible and efficient Python implementations. To address this, a Generalized Graphical Lasso (GGLasso) objective was formulated, from which the standard Graphical Lasso object can be derived as a specific case. A new, flexible Python library called GGLasso has been created to efficiently calculate the GGLasso object using the Coordinate Descent algorithm.

Numerous simulation techniques are utilized in computer science to assess complex structures, particularly in determining the stability of large molecular structures. One such structure is RNA, which when combined into large assemblies, exhibits potential applications in medicine and biology but also faces challenges in maintaining stability due to internal forces. A critical issue is identifying feasible molecular configurations capable of sustaining intended functions, although current methods struggle with efficiency in finding multiple feasible configurations simultaneously. This study presents an innovative molecular dynamics approach, ConfiguLa, designed to efficiently generate a set of feasible configurations at once. By integrating constraints into the Langevin dynamics model, ConfiguLa achieves a robust performance in sampling configurations for complex molecular structures, particularly in complex RNA assemblies. The results indicate that ConfiguLa outperforms the standard methods in generating diverse and high-quality configurations within a short simulation time frame, ultimately providing a reliable foundation for designing functional and efficient molecular structures.

This research builds upon a previous gravitational potential simulation, which considered the effects of a supermassive black hole on the dispersion of electromagnetic pulses around it. Now, the current study incorporates the wave shadow phenomenon, the distortion of images caused by the black hole, and adds the interaction of two black holes to the simulation. The new program, written in Fortran, delivers updated results that consider the wave shadow effect and the merger of two black holes of differing masses within the same simulation environment. The outcomes show that the wave shadow phenomenon has a noticeable impact, particularly when one black hole is significantly larger than the other, resulting in a distorted matter distribution in the final simulation. The results are illustrated with color maps representing the logarithm of the total mass density of the surrounding cloud, along with orbital trajectories of particle tracers, which can be easily integrated into the simulation from the previous simulation available for download on the same server.

Consider an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam consisting of a central beam connected to $N$ additional outer beams at an internal node, where the outer beams are supported by dampers at their free ends. The system's asymptotic stability under initial conditions with compact support is analyzed, taking into consideration various angles of the outer beams and the forces transmitted between the central beam and outer beams. A key finding is the existence of a stability threshold, associated with the angles of the outer beams, below which the system's energy decays at a rate of $1/\sqrt{t}$. The paper proves that the system's energy conforms to this threshold, adopting the threshold's characteristics. Furthermore, the proof is strengthened to accounts for situations where the beam's angles approach their equilibrium positions.

Researchers in photoacoustic tomography often encounter difficulties with the varying speeds of sound in tissues, which can distort data and reduce the quality of images. To improve image resolution, research into special acoustic lenses with high speed-of-sound materials has been active. However, the suitable materials needed are rare, expensive, and prone to corrosion or degradation over time. To address these issues, this research introduces a novel acoustic lens substance called poly(vinyl alcohol), exhibiting a desired high speed of sound while being biocompatible, biodegradable, and durable. Further studies, along with simulations and experiments, demonstrate its effectiveness in enhancing the detection range of large array detectors and providing uniform concentration improvements of roughly 1.47 times.

Community detection and node classification are fundamental issues in the fields of network analysis and related fields such as data mining. Recent breakthroughs in this area have involved the development of prominent methods like graph prominence and vector prominence. However, these approaches have not fully considered the complexities of multilayer networks, which consist of multiple interconnected networks linked through corresponding nodes. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of K-layer prominence, a method that integrates the relationships between the component networks to provide a more nuanced understanding of node importance and classification within multilayer networks. The novelty of our approach lies in the derivation of prominence values through a process that combines the application of Laplacian operators to each of the K constituent networks. A key innovation of our model is the use of outer product matrices to explore the interconnected relationships between the K components, thereby enabling prominence values to reflect both the intrinsic properties of each network and their interdependent relationships. To validate our model, we conducted experiments on multilayer networks obtained from real-world datasets, and the results indicate that node classifications derived from our prominence values exhibit significant improvements over those achieved using traditional methods.

Previous research on deblurring, demosaicing and denoising has mainly targeted individual tasks, using artificial or pre-processed data to train models, which does not accurately reflect the actual data captured by the camera's sensor. This work differs by directly dealing with motion blur, color demosaicing and shot noise in images simultaneously in a single step. We designed and executed an experiment on two types of cameras, using real images with controlled noise and blur, and collaborated with deblurring experts to test our method across a range of camera settings and blur levels. We developed a end-to-end model to demosaic and denoise raw images in a single step, and trained it on artificially blurred and noised data. Interestingly, this single-step model also outperformed the collaboration approach for certain settings. We designed and executed it on two types of cameras, and conducted experiments on real images with controlled noise and blur, to demonstrate our result.

Using the techniques of scalar field algebraic quantization, we successfully derive the Dirac operator within a specific star product associated with deformed Minkowski spacetime, utilizing the deformed S-matrix approach. This achievement showcases that our method can also achieve $C$-parity invariance. Furthermore, we obtain the full spectrum of the derived Dirac operator.

These tools are also referred to as Bayesian networks, where the structure represents the set of edges in a DGA. The process of structure learning can be done through various methods, but the choice of method is crucial, as different approaches yield varying results. The Causal Exploration Toolbox (CAT) is designed to provide a range of Bayesian structure learning methods, with the ability to perform multiple trials and compare the outcomes. The CAT is particularly useful for visualizing complex systems, with a focus on the set of edges that define the relationships between variables. The CAT is essential for a deeper understanding of the causal structure, with the ability to generate the DAGA visual representation. To understand how entries of soft viscoelastic fluids change due to their elasticity and fatiguing, we investigated nonNewtonian, spherical entries and found that at lower velocities, a surface seal forms, which also appears in viscoelastic fluids.  However, as the sphere enters faster, the necking instability shifts from the sphere to the stem.  A new, more robust limit for moderate entry speeds is also defined by a modeled relationship between the sphere's radius, elasticity force, and the fluid's viscosity.

In a well-studied category of Type IIB string theory compactifications, often called "large complex structure" (LCS), the model features an abundance of superfluous moduli. These extra degrees of freedom can lead to unmanageably large vacuum energies due to the decoupling of two-dimensional states. To address this problem, a particular class of theories was analyzed, in which many of these moduli are unified under a single symmetry-breaking mechanism, enabling some states to transform into two heavy states. Furthermore, it was discovered that certain "fractional instantons" may allow for the extension of nonperturbative effects, allowing for a more manageable vacuum configuration. However, these instantonic effects must be carefully balanced against other two-loop corrections to maintain a stable vacuum. As a result, certain supersymmetric potentials can achieve a stable, negative cosmological constant while preserving at least one fermionic supercharge, or an effective V=0 with an additional field. Ultimately, it was shown that certain UV-completed theories can allow for an infinite expansion of these instantonic effects, enabling a stable vacuum configuration, but such scenarios are rare among all possible LCS theories.

Recent advances in confidence estimation for deep neural networks (DNNs) hold much promise in assessing the reliability of critical applications during operation. Nevertheless, these methods primarily rely on additional hardware for enhanced confidence measurement, thereby incurring significant cost increases. In this paper, we explore the feasibility of utilizing confidence estimation methods that do not require any extra hardware resources, even in settings where the underlying DNN generates highly accurate outputs. Our research reveals that current confidence estimation methods fail to provide reliable results with only internal feedback. Consequently, we introduce two innovative approaches based solely on the DNN's own predictions and the data input. Our evaluations across multiple benchmarks indicate consistent, precise confidence estimates that correlate strongly with actual performance, all without needing any supplementary hardware.

known to be vulnerable to sophisticated cyber-attacks that mislead them by
manipulating input data. A new type of attack has emerged, however, which is
on par with the best flawed training data and leads to models that are doomed
to failure no matter what counter-measures are implemented. We now face the
critical challenge of preventing such disaster. We propose a solution in the
form of the Resilient Policy Gradient method, which is capable of overcoming
this issue. Our approach prevents the adverse counter-measure strategy from
being adopted by the attacker and ensures that the model's counter-measuring
capability is not compromised. We establish the optimal cost of this
resilient model and provide a mathematical proof of its optimality. We also
introduce the concept of the resilience gap, which measures the difference
between the model's optimal cost and that of an ideal model that is trained
without regard to security. We further introduce the concept of the secure
optimal counter-measuring strategy, which is the best counter-measure the
model can anticipate in response to the adverse counter-measure strategy. We
show that the model's resilient training is equivalent to learning the secure
optimal counter-measure and provide the formulation of the resilient model's
value function. We also introduce the resilient policy gradient method as our
solution. We also provide the mathematical proof that the resilient policy

In the context of the box game, we examine a variation where players are randomly matched and rewarded with either $1 or $0 based on a predetermined probability. Introducing "selection" into the traditional model, we utilize a large-scale simulation to explore how the game's outcome changes. Our simulation reveals that the traditional model leads to a selection dilemma where the majority of the population tends to avoid playing, as the benefit of selection exceeds a certain threshold. Interestingly, our results also show that in the variation where randomly selected individuals are always rewarded $1, selection eventually drives the majority of the population to participate in the game.

Cubanite, a 3d transition metal sulfide with a particular crystal structure, exhibits multiple physical properties including pyromagnetism, a changing specific heat anomaly, and notable magnetic anisotropy. Our study uses a combination of theoretical and experimental methods to investigate the material's magnetic structure and orbital configuration. By comparing experiments to theoretical models, we found that the oxygen-like crystal field caused by the sulfide environment creates self-consistent occupied d-x-y and virtual d-z^2 orbitals for the iron ions within the material. The self-energy spectrum obtained through X-ray absorption spectroscopy in the first-principles + GWA approach illustrates virtual excitations aligned with the eg and t2g crystal field states. Furthermore, our research reveals that the ferromagnetic order is virtual due to self-interaction and many-body effects, and the uniaxial anisotropy is primarily generated by the d-z^2 electron density concentrated near the iron ion poles. By placing cubanite in a quantum self-consistent description, our work provides a fundamental understanding of its self-interacting electronic and magnetic behavior and suggests that it may serve as an ideal benchmark material.

A remarkable phenomenon, autonomous Rabi oscillations, occurs when a pair of photons induces periodic swaps of an exciton's state between bright and dark forms without the need for a magnetic field. Through careful experimentation, we demonstrate that dark excitons participate in Rabi oscillations by measuring their phase evolution using a variant known as area resonance. The oscillations' speed and nature are determined by a balance of interactions involving the exciton, its surrounding crystal lattice, and nearby photons. Our results lay the foundation for developing quantum technologies based on semi-neutral particles and provide a method to investigate the complex dynamics of dark matter.

In two-dimensional non-symmorphic wallpaper groups, there's a rich variety of lattice structures that allow for extensive exploration of lattice physics beyond simple symmorphic groups. This paper focuses on constructing Hamiltonians for four representative two-dimensional non-symmorphic wallpaper group lattices using a basis of minimal supercells, and identifies Dirac points in Hamiltonians for space group P2$_2$$_2$ and its time-reversal partner, space group P2$_2$$_2$$_m$. Furthermore, it shows that the position of these Dirac points is adjustable, and the non-symmorphic nature of the lattice enables unusual topological properties, such as large topological charge values and multiple Chern band repetitions, in contrast to one-atom-unit and mirror symmetries in some non-symmorphic 2D space groups that hinder topological characteristics.

A novel type of quantum state known as single-photon facilitated coherent state (SFCS) is introduced, which is effectively generated using quantum-optical catalysis. These SFCSs can be viewed as damped versions of standard coherent states, modified by an exponential suppression factor representing the probability of admitting exactly one photon. Quantum-optical catalysis serves as a efficient method in achieving this state through post-selection, while maintaining the benefit of utilizing all detected photons. As a result, the SFCS embodies some of the key quantum features typical of coherent states but to a lesser extent. Furthermore, entanglement within these states can be explicitly calculated, and it is found that they possess measurable super- and sub-Poissonian characteristics. Their decay rates and average decay times are determined and found to resemble those of standard coherent states. Additionally, their suitability in quantum communication protocols, particularly in phase-anti-phase discrimination, is评估ed and it is determined that they retain significant performance in such applications.

In General Relativity, using the Newman-Penrose formalism provides a convenient way to work with antisymmetric tensors like the Maxwell field $F_{ab}$ and Weyl curvature $C_{abcd}$. By leveraging the NP framework and employing a null tetrad, complex scalians are derived from these tensors through contraction, following the standard convention from reference [1]. To extend this analysis, the GRTensorII package is utilized to generate null quadradads and compute the corresponding NP scalars, using examples of Maxwell fields and Weyl curvatures in global coordinates. Specifically, a Melvin magnetic field is examined as a case study.

Predicting how polymers behave is challenging due to their complex molecular structure and the intricate balance of intermolecular forces that shape their properties. This complexity often necessitates experimenting with numerous samples to establish reliable structure-property relationships, which can be time-consuming and costly. Our novel computational approach aims to uncover these relationships by analyzing data from molecular dynamics simulations for liquids made up of Star-Henry type polymers. By applying a linear regression method to this data, even an imperfect strategy like this can successfully reveal the essential structure-property relationships within such systems. This method ultimately leads to a clearer understanding of how molecular structure influences polymer behavior.

Immediate Transcription is an innovative method for creating high-fidelity simulations that incorporate real-time data from the physical world. Typically utilized to supplement existing high-fidelity simulations, this method has rarely been explored in the context of dynamic systems affecting human behavior and social interactions. With advancements in AI and machine learning coming of age, immediate transcription has the potential to be applied to a wider range of scenarios, including those involving human interactions. With breathing sounds from two individuals possibly infected with COVID- nearby as an example, this paper examines how immediate transcription can be implemented using a system that analyzes audio signals. By modifying existing high-fidelity simulations and incorporating real-time data from audio recordings, this paper explores how breathing sounds can influence human perceptions, even in the absence of visual cues. An experimental investigation with human participants has further validated the efficacy of this method.

Neoplasms, unwanted tumor masses, can spread rapidly and metastasize, 
making early detection via accurate imaging analysis crucial for successful 
treatment. Next-generation AI techniques are being developed to seamlessly 
integrate with radiologists' workflows by delivering exceptionally precise 
segmentations of neoplasms in medical images. In this study, we present an AI 
model capable of accurately segmenting neoplasms in CT scans, capable of 
processing low-resolution images and delivering excellent performance even in 
challenging cases where neoplasms occupy a small portion of the image. The DDUnet 
architecture features an expanded Dense Unet structure with focus layers that 
produce high-quality segmentations by fusing slices across the CT scan's length. 
The model's training is guided by heavy similarity metrics that account for 
neighborhood similarities across images and neoplasms, as well as focal 
similarity between predicted and target focus masks. Furthermore, the proposed 
method is among the first to accurately identify and segment 3D neoplasms in CT 
scans at endoscopic views without accompanying mask data.

Our novel approach uses a flexible framework that models log measurements through basic building blocks, providing a means to evaluate the reliability of the results. This method, which isn't solely dependent on Bayesian assumptions, enables the incorporation of diverse constraints and yields estimates of parameter uncertainties, crucial for geosteering decisions. We developed a basic suite of framework tools using the LangChain and Scikit-learn frameworks, capable of extending into more advanced machine learning methodologies. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a case study on the appraisal well A-40A of the A block in the Gulf of Mexico, where the framework assesses log data uncertainties to refine reservoir property estimates, ultimately informing geosteering decisions.

Nested named entity recognition, a challenging task on par with other complex NLP problems like nested relation classification and nested text simplification, can be viewed as identifying named entities within a document's overall hierarchy. This paper proposes a simple yet effective approach to nested NER, focusing on analyzing a document's holistic structure. By combining character-level and document-level components, our model processes input data and identifies named entities by assessing the document's global architecture. Notably, our system achieves state-of-the-art results on two prominent evaluation datasets, CHNER and Fine-grained WIKI.

We'll examine the connections between rational and tropical geometry in the context of a smooth complex quartic surface without singularities. A recent study by Guo and Xu has established a method to compute the number of a quartic surface's tropicalization's smooth points in a way that correlates with its A1-count over the original surface's rational points. We've discovered that the tropical points' combinatorial data can be linked to their rational points' A1-count through a specific weighting system. A key theoretical framework, the Nahm-Schopp interface, allows us to utilize this link to demonstrate the equality of their rational and tropical counting methods. We assume a technical condition to prove the rational counting of the surface's bitangent planes matches its tropical counterpart's count. These bitangent planes' relationships to the surface's tangent planes at two points share a specific property, where their intersection lines form a special type of curve known as a rational normal quartic. The approach used to prove this result can be adapted under broader conditions, as long as the surface's defining equation meets certain criteria.

This research focuses on locating a set of target nodes within a wireless sensor network using a two-dimensional coordinate system. We consider scenarios where GPS-enabled reference nodes and ordinary communication nodes transmit and receive signals, and these signals may be disrupted by unsynchronized, high-power transmissions from a mobile device operating on an incompatible frequency. A new algorithm is developed to handle this type of noise, allowing for precise target node localization. We test and evaluate the performance of this algorithm through simulations using a customized NS-2 module. Results show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, delivering sub-meter target node locations with GPS node spacing as small as 10 meters. We also investigate the effect of increasing noise power on localization performance.

Code-switching, the interweaving of two or more languages within a single utterance, poses significant communication challenges but is also prevalent among Generation Z across various age groups and languages. Numerous studies have explored code-switching, yet they primarily focus on monolingual speech. In contrast, multilingual speech presents additional obstacles due to multiple factors, including the number of languages involved, their structural similarities, and the societal status of each language. This code-based distinction sets multilingual speech apart from monolingual speech, for which existing NLP models for classification, translation, and other tasks are extensively available. To bridge this gap, a comprehensive overview of code-switched or multilingual speech is presented, encompassing its underlying theories, NLP task challenges, current models, and a genealogical genealogy of multilingual speech. This research aims to pave the way for future developments in NLP models for code-switched or multilingual speech.

Evaluating the accuracy of automatically generated image descriptions is a crucial aspect of this technology. Currently, commonly used methods involve comparing automated subtitles to human-written references, either individually or in combination. However, considering that multiple human observers can provide varying descriptions of the same image, each with its own set of strengths and weaknesses, simply treating all human references as perfectly reliable may lead to biased evaluation metrics. In an effort to develop a more precise method for assessing automatic image descriptions, we investigate a model that utilizes human reference information by incorporating uncertainty associated with the provided descriptions. In experiments conducted on two widely used datasets, this approach has been shown to have superior predictive capabilities compared to traditional methods.

Our first-principles and Monte Carlo investigations into the Ta$_2$O$_5$ paracrystalline phase have yielded the structure parameters matching experimental measurements. By minimizing total energy, the Ta$_2$O$_5$ base state crystal structure was theoretically described for the first time. Additional simulations have also provided Ta$_2$O$_5$ amorphous phase structure parameters.

Geographic segregation on the internet may exacerbate polarization by limiting exposure to differing viewpoints and promoting misinformation dissemination. Reddit's community structure, which spans multiple states, is designed to reduce this effect by facilitating exposure to diverse perspectives beyond a single state. This study examines the role of geographic segregation in the spread of misinformation within Reddit communities, utilizing Reddit elections pages as case examples. It reveals that although geographic arrangement contributes to increased misinformation propagation, the design of more than a single column can mitigate this effect. Furthermore, it reveals that users located in geographic regions unfamiliar with the predominant viewpoint as determined by the arrangement, experience increased exposure to minority viewpoints and information ambiguity. As a result, they are less convinced that the majority opinion represents the genuine public stance. Nonetheless, implementing more than a single column can elicit discomfort with ambiguity, leading users to seek out supporting evidence for preferred views. This finding suggests that Reddit users' preference for single-column setups may serve an adaptive purpose, facilitating effective misinformation management within online discussions.

The escalating speed of online information has sparked interest in manually processing news events in real-time, especially during major occurrences like earthquakes, terrorist attacks, and natural disasters. Event detection systems aim to automatically track and differentiate between significant occurrences and daily occurrences. However, these systems struggle with certain categories like crimes, explosions, and protests due to their ambiguous nature. To better understand this problem, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of large-scale datasets from diverse social media platforms by creating summary graphs that visually represent the evolution of topics over time. This visual representation facilitated our exploration into topics with unreliable labels, leading us to propose a classification framework based on three primary features extracted from these summary graphs. To classify dubious events, we employed a diverse range of machine learning models, with our top-performing system combining BERT and a Dobbs-based rule, exceeding human accuracy in our comprehensive evaluation across topics, data sources, and event durations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive study on dubious events across multiple platforms in a real-world setting, which we hope will provide valuable insights for future research.

Humans frequently employ gestures and language when teaching skills to others by demonstration. Adding verbal commentary to manipulation tasks taught through imitation could enhance the learning process for robots. However, our current understanding of how humans structure verbal feedback during such tasks is limited. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap. We recorded experts performing pickup and placement tasks alongside verbal explanations. The verbal explanations were then analyzed categorically and sequentially. The results revealed that during tasks involving one object, exophoric expressions are used to refer to the object, while during tasks with multiple objects, definite descriptions are used. Furthermore, the verbal commentary is aligned with the task at hand, using expressions that facilitate the comprehension of the task. This understanding of how humans structure verbal feedback during manipulation tasks will enable the development of more effective communication strategies between humans and robots during task execution.

The prevalence of random tree generation algorithms is limited, despite their potential utility in areas like computer networking, algorithm analysis, and various mathematical studies. These studies frequently require the examination of specific random tree models, including those with binary connections or the ability to accommodate varying degrees of connection at each node. In this study, I present a systematic approach to creating random trees that can be applied to any specified network. This methodology includes the development of three distinct tree generation algorithms, along with proof of their output's statistical independence. Additionally, I demonstrate the value of this method through its use in producing simulation data for the investigation of binary search tree performance in scenarios involving massive data updates.

Our research reveals a complex relationship between geometric field theory and Euler-Arnold equations, revealing a comparable complication. To illustrate this, we adapt a concept from gauge field theory and geometric field theory to create a geometric analog of the Chern-Simons action. Subsequently, we derive the associated Euler-Lagrange equations. Finally, we impose standard mean field approximations on geometric probabilistic fields, resulting in a complex analogous relationship between geometric field theory and quantum mechanics.

The concept of a conversational agent, commonly known as a chatbot, has
long been studied, but the advent of deep learning models such as ASR and NLU
has sparked significant interest in the establishment of a universally accepted
conversational system and its evaluation. Despite the diverse nature of
applications, the current landscape lacks a unified framework for the automated
assessment of these systems. Our evaluation framework is designed to
systematically compare human-human interactions with those facilitated by
conversational agents, providing a comprehensive metric for their performance.
This evaluation methodology is straightforward to execute and encompasses
essential aspects of human communication, namely, semantic understanding,
language generation, and contextual coherence. To our knowledge, this is the
initial attempt at establishing a unified evaluation standard for
conversational agents, paving the way for heightened excitement and excitement
in the field.

Our methodology involves placing virtual objects, which we term "Planet X" candidates, in various orbits within the solar system and assessing their gravitational impact on the present-day tracking of the known planets. By using the Jet Propulsion Laboratory's planetary ephemeris as a reference, we measure the resulting discrepancies or "residuals" in the observations. These virtual objects are then detected if their presence significantly improves the fit of the observations to the data. We illustrate this process by attempting to discover a fifth giant planet in the solar system and determine the minimum mass required for it to be detected using the present method. The method's ability to discover additional solar system objects is primarily limited by the number of objects that can be statistically distinguished from the main belt population in the phase space of mass and semi-major axis.
