Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low multipole harmonies and 'cold spots', could be remnants of events from a previous universe in the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology theory. To test this hypothesis, we developed a more comprehensive statistical analysis to detect such signatures. Our findings so far have not provided strong evidence for the CCC's predictions, although a further, more detailed analysis of the CMB has not yielded contradictory results. We also explored the idea of using machine learning techniques to enhance our analysis and discovered that models trained to distinguish between dark energy and CCC hypotheses have shown the capability of accurately differentiating between them, predominantly in favor of the dark energy model. We also made improvements to the simulated data used in our simulations to better reflect the actual observations, thus strengthening our analysis.

This study builds upon an earlier work of the authors by addressing the convergence of the Yamabe flow, a dynamic version of the Yamabe flow, under specific initial conditions. A key property of the Yamabe flow is the uniform boundness of the Yamabe constant across all time. To prove convergence, the flow's behavior must be analyzed further. Building on the existing framework, the current research expands the applicable initial data for which the convergence occurs. For more details on the Yamabe flow, please refer to the corresponding author's publication.

To efficiently adapt to new tasks without retraining models, prototype-based networks utilize a storage mechanism to learn features and a matching mechanism to apply that knowledge. However, traditional approaches use individual sample features, not necessarily effective, and only work well for single-class learning. By incorporating class-level prototypes, we can enhance the prototyping module's performance on multi-class tasks. In response, we propose an innovative approach that combines an effective feature selection module with a novel prototype learning module. Our method initially generates descriptors for each category using only a few samples and refines these descriptions through a new multi-shot prototype refinement module. It then acquires precise class-level prototypes from these descriptions. To facilitate data efficiency, we also introduce a novel multi-view consistency module that leverages multiple descriptions to create accurate prototypes. The proposed method also employs only a small amount of training data, not the entire dataset, to refine these prototypes. We validate our method's efficacy through comprehensive evaluations, demonstrating superior results compared to leading methods. We release our models to aid future research.

To enhance cross-domain recommendation systems, we propose a novel, comprehensive aspect-preference learning framework that leverages cooperative information from multiple sparse domains. This framework's key innovation lies in its ability to capture hidden, multifaceted user preferences by integrating data from each individual sparse domain, as well as their hidden interactions within each domain and across multiple domains. A significant challenge we encounter is the issue of conflicting information, which hinders the learning of user preferences due to the lack of domain consistency. To address this, we've designed a refined aspect-preference learning model that (1) decomposes user preferences into separate, independent components for each domain, and multiple latent components that capture their hidden interactions, and (2) leverages an adaptive weighting mechanism to resolve conflicts of information by assigning adaptive weights to each component according to its informational value for user preference estimation. Experimental evaluations on real-world data sets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method, which exhibits superior performance compared to existing multi-domain recommendation approaches.

Organic conic optimization holds much promise in solving complex engineering and scientific optimization problems. However, modeling tools often fall short due to limited conic adaptation and undocumented default settings in popular formats like AMPL, GPKN, and JuMP. These issues hinder the efficient resolution of nontrivial organic conic optimization problems. To overcome these challenges, we present Hypatia as an all-inclusive package for formulating and optimizing such problems using the JuMP ecosystem in Julia. Leveraging the rich capabilities of differential algebraic equations, the package automatically converts organic conic optimization problems into second-order cone programs, facilitating their swift and accurate solution by the GLPK Simplex Algorithm or the Interior Point Method. We illustrate the package's capabilities in two computationally intensive applications: reconstructing historical Roman acoustic acoustic design and resolving complex vortex flow dynamics, the latter being a benchmark problem in fluid dynamics.

Using artificial intelligence for medical image analysis relies on a large number of high-quality labeled training samples to ensure the models work effectively for new, unlabeled images. Some studies attempted to circumvent the need for manual labeling by using self-supervised learning. These methods used neural networks to learn the basic characteristics of medical images. However, this approach only ensures the models can process new, unlabeled images. It doesn't guarantee they can accurately identify pathologies. Due to a significant gap in research on using self-supervised learning for medical imaging, it's crucial to investigate the underlying reasons. One key issue discovered is that methods which claim to generalize well across domains, in fact, struggle with the variety of conditions present in medical images, and are instead limited to handling a small number of typical cases. This limitation is exacerbated by the fact that data from different scanners often contain different characteristic features, which methods focusing on extracting implicit data representations fail to handle cleanly. This study proposes an innovative method called Model-Agnostic Denoising Reference Learning, which directly addresses this problem. It's applied to multiple types of medical imaging studies, yielding models which perform at least as well as traditional self-supervised learning approaches when combined with a small number of labeled images.

The adoption of privately owned electric vehicles can significantly influence the resilience of electrical distribution networks during disruptions. This impact depends on how EV owners use their vehicles and prioritize various objectives, such as maximizing mobility, reducing energy costs, and maintaining grid stability. To address this complex issue, a novel multi-objective optimization approach was created to balance these competing interests and enhance overall system resilience. The proposed approach formulates the problem as a game between EV users and grid operators, which can be resolved through a backward-induction strategy. To efficiently solve the complex equations involved, a pioneering method was developed that combines genetic algorithms with the primal-dive method. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the proposed solution was demonstrated through the creation of a probability-based operation plan for EVs, along with numerical examples and a discussion of the method's computational performance and the EVs' impact on grid resilience.

In cloud-based machine learning workflows and extensive database operations, transient computing platforms depend on non-volatile storage solutions, transferring large datasets between external devices and main memory. Current research has explored various persistent memory technologies to replace traditional disk-based storage. This paper presents an in-depth examination of the Intel Optane DC Persistent Storage Module's capabilities, using a range of custom-designed applications. Our tests reveal that data can be efficiently transferred from the Optane Module to CPU RAM within under five milliseconds using a customized version of the XPB protocol. Furthermore, our research is limited by its use of a standalone Optane Module. To overcome this limitation, an extension to the XPB protocol is proposed, which would allow Optane Modules to be directly managed by the CPU, potentially reducing latency to less than one millisecond.

Advanced Driving Assistance Systems and Self-driving technologies comprise a diverse array of meticulously engineered components that vary by capability, including lane keeping, braking, and navigation. These components interact in complex ways in real-world traffic scenarios, presenting both cooperative and competitive dynamics. In this study, a new framework is presented that enables multi-agent recurrent safe meeting via a step-by-step incentive model learned through deep reinforcement learning. Agents in this framework apply a learned policy in each stage of a stage-based Markov decision process to achieve a collision-free rendezvous. The result is an efficient framework capable of coordinating multiple agents in reaching a safe meeting, as demonstrated with simulated tests involving three cooperative autonomous vehicles in a multi-lane highway scenario.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) through first-principles calculations. Our study shows that CmSn3 and the GdxCm1-xSn3 series are stable against volume changes and that CmSn3 and GdSn3 exhibit the same rock-salt crystal structure. Both materials as well as the GdxCm1-xSn3 series show promise as topological materials with distinct characteristics. Our calculations indicate that GdSn3 and the GdxCm1-xSn3 series have strong magnetic moments centered on the rare earth atoms. Moreover, GdSn3 and the GdxCm1-xSn3 series have zoom-in features in their density of states near the Fermi level, a hallmark of topological materials. Additionally, our study finds that the magnetic moment in GdSn3 and the GdxCm1-xSn3 series closely follows the Ziman rule.

According to the Standard Model of particle physics and observations from the Cosmic Microwave Background, there should be roughly ten times more dark matter than normal (baryonic) matter in the universe. This model of matter allows for density fluctuations on small scales, potentially enabling massive clumps of baryonic matter, or "extra Galaxies," that mimic the appearance of dark matter-dominated galaxies during observations. Furthermore, under highly suppressed conditions, fluctuations could lead to the formation of non-baryonic and baryonic mesons, or "mesoballs," through the direct application of Gravitational Wave spectroscopy to the Big Bang. However, these mesoballs would be unstable and quickly break down into normal matter particles.
The foundation theorem for Coxeter groups of type B has been generalized to include all standard parabolic subgroups of type B.

Utilizing an external gravitational lens, we determine the distance to distant supernovae beyond the range observable directly, an technique anticipated to significantly enhance the precision of Hubble constant ($H_0$) measurements. Data from three distinct surveys which compiled the Pantheon $S$N Ia dataset in 2019 provide the first comprehensive analysis of the feasibility of image distortion patterns, or shear patterns, around 100 $S$N Ia within the Pantheon dataset in the redshift range between $0.1 < z < 0.9$. Based on these observations we predict utilizing the Euclid and COSMO-2020 surveys we could identify shear patterns around 10 to 30 $S$N Ia breaking the degeneracies of $H_0$ and $\Omega_0$ parameters within the $\Lambda$CDM model.
These are the written contributions to the introduction to stochastic partial differential equations session at the University of Edinburgh in September 2021.

In modern data centers, network infrastructure relies heavily on optical interconnects to handle increasing traffic demands efficiently. However, routing complexities in two-dimensional chip surfaces limit routing capabilities, necessitating a shift to three-dimensional (3D) chip arrangements. Introducing 3D optical interconnects introduces new challenges in designing and optimizing T-shaped couplers that route signals across multiple directions. We investigated various T-hub designs using silicon-on-insulator (SOI) materials, evaluating them based on insertion loss, crosstalk, and bandwidth. Our studies revealed that ideal T-hubs with 10 dB insertion loss, less than -30 dB crosstalk, and a bandwidth exceeding 100 GHz can be realized when all arms are of equal length. Furthermore, we demonstrated that integrating 2D/3D optical interconnects using T-hubs as switches can create reconfigurable networks capable of supporting both two and four-dimensional routing needs. These capabilities pave the way for developing 2D and 3D optical interconnects with switch-closed loops that support optimal, complex network configurations.

This letter examines the effects of three manipulation techniques used in MRI
images - Gaussian blur, contrast adjustment, and Gaussian noise - on the performance
of a Deep Learning-based detection model. By investigating these techniques individually
and in combination, we aim to determine their impact on the model's ability to
accurately detect tumors in MRI scans.

Our experiments reveal that while a solitary altered technique may not significantly
impair detection performance, the presence of multiple altered techniques can lead to
substantial declines in performance. Notably, our research also demonstrates that
these manipulated techniques can be reversed, enabling a straightforward restoration
of the original image and consequent enhancement of detection performance.

Our findings suggest that a deep learning model, once trained, can still effectively
operate on previously manipulated images, provided the detection task isn't excessively
complex. This also highlights the critical role of data preprocessing, including
image restoration, in ensuring optimal deep learning performance.

To support future research, we have made our dataset and processing code available
online, facilitating advancements in tumor detection using machine learning models.

The classical approach by K. Eiseniskis for computationally determining Bernoulli numbers involves extensive calculations with large integers. In contrast, K. Ohshita introduced a K-theoretic approach yielding analogous values using computations with polynomials instead. This algebraic method's advantage lies in its scalability, as it facilitates deriving computations for higher-values from previous results. We will demonstrate this relation and further extend it to p-adic values using Bernoulli-Kato polynomials. Additionally, we'll establish a new formula connecting Chow groups of moduli spaces with products of Bernoulli polynomials.

In astronomy, spectral analysis is hindered by changes in celestial activity, which affect a star's spectrum and reduce the signal quality. To mitigate this issue, we need to select line collections that are resistant to such fluctuations. This research focuses on understanding how line collections, whether parametric or randomly chosen, affect the outcomes of deconvolution. A comprehensive set of 51555 HIPPARCS5 hydrogen lines was used to experiment with different line collections and determine the optimal configuration for deconvolution. The results showed that certain hydrogen lines in the UV range have a natural tendency to cluster together and, when used, can significantly improve the quality of the deconvolved spectra. Moreover, adding more lines to the collections did not always lead to better outcomes. These findings can be applied to experiments with line collections made from other types of atoms. Ultimately, we found that line combinations with a large number of hydrogen lines in the near-UV range, particularly those in the PSPR (Pressure Shifted Paschen series) series, have the potential to reduce atmospheric noise and reduce the need for large telescopes for high-precision velocity measurements.

Recent protocols in Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) have reduced energy usage during data collection missions by organizing nodes into logical groups, known as scope sectors, that define a node's hierarchical relationship with other nodes. Although the concept of hierarchical grouping has been around for some time, defining the hierarchy between nodes has not been widely explored. To address this gap, we introduce a novel approach called Hierarchy, Scope, and Integrity Estimation (HSIE), a bidirectional grouping method using Virtual Carrier Sensing (VCS). In HSEI, nodes determine their hierarchy with neighboring nodes, thus creating a complete graph where the direction of the link represents the hierarchical relationship. To illustrate the effectiveness of HSIE, we developed a P4J simulation, comparing its performance with existing scope sectorization methods, such as HSS-DOGE and DOGE-WSN, in terms of energy efficiency, task completion speed, and link integrity. Our results show that HSIE outperforms comparable methods, offering a robust and efficient solution for data collection in WSNs.

Our research introduces a context-aware scoring mechanism for objects that are not fully observable, such as cars, trains, and other entities, by combining context-free and context-aware feature extraction methods. This context-aware scoring mechanism is capable of achieving impressive results in complex detection scenarios, even without trained category-specific features. It surpasses the performance of context-ignoring scoring systems and context-free UltraNet in context-sensitive category tasks, as evidenced by our experiments across a range of entities. Furthermore, our context-aware scoring mechanism shows remarkable versatility and versatility across an extensive collection of 400 objects in the UltraRecall benchmark, outshining current SOTA methods that do not consider contextual elements. It is also crucial to highlight that context-aware scoring mechanism can be easily applied to a broad range of categories beyond the scope of the UltraRecall benchmark.

This study examines multiple indefinite Kirchhoff-type elliptic equations that combine singular interactions and Trudinger-Moser-type growth nonlinearity. By applying a critical approximation technique and minimax arguments, we establish both compact and non-compact solution branches. Subsequently, an isolated branch of solutions is shown to exhibit blowup behavior as a parameter approaches its limit value.

Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent binary random variables that converge in distribution to a Poisson random variable, with their covariance matrix being positive semidefinite and having entries representing the product of $-X_i$ and $-X_j$. We examine the concentration properties of the sum of these random variables, with a specific focus on how concentration varies among the variables in the sum.

Recently, related concepts to Fontaine-Messing theory have been explored in power series algebras by the first author and Sköldberg. This new framework is not as fully developed as its CRPF analogue, but it still offers a partial converse to the Fontaine-Messing theorem within power series algebras, albeit with a notably simpler and more accessible proof than its counterpart in characteristic zero. Furthermore, this current work aims to fill in the remaining gaps in the reference provided by the original author and skoldberg.

The proposed analysis of dihadron data from semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering using longitudinally polarized electrons off an unpolarized proton target can serve as a powerful tool for investigating the spin structure of the proton. This process is particularly sensitive to the correlation between the spin of the proton and the transverse momentum of the hadrons produced. To increase statistical significance, considering the azimuthal angle of the second hadron relative to the first hadron's momentum, or the product of the azimuthal angles of both hadrons, can prove beneficial. To better understand the contributions from different processes, next-to-leading order QCD corrections need to be taken into account, which can be essential for accurate predictions in SIDIS data, unlike the leading order predictions that often suffice.

We've developed a method to calculate the average entropy density in the universe's vacuum state, finding that it aligns with the non-renormalized entropy density in a two-dimensional de Sitter space. This connection holds true when considering the gravitational fields in a form that corresponds to the non-gravitational case. The value of this entropy density is directly related to Fock's concept of the metric's Hilbert space from 1957, though it diverges from his calculated value. Specifically, our calculation yields a result that is four times his initial calculation of the determinant of the Fock-Neri matrix.

Let Y be a symplectic manifold with a fixed symplectic structure denoted by $\omega$. If the symplectic form $\omega$ can be transformed into another form $\omega'$ that is also symplectic, but not equivalent to the original through a smooth symplectic transformation, we say that $\omega'$ is a symplectic modification of $\omega$ on Y. In this article, we will explore the main characteristics of such symplectic modifications and provide an overview of the primary examples of such situations.

To automatically generate entities for Wikipedia articles, a straightforward yet effective approach is to utilize the Wikipedia–WikiData–Yahoo! Knowledge Graph (WKWD). To integrate this resource, we developed a method to embed dictionaries from Wikipedia and WikiData into layered graphs. This involves representing hyperlinks as edges and applying Hopfield Neural Networks (HNN) to infer missing information. By incorporating HNN, our proposed model, Layered Diagram Embedding for Entity Suggestion (LENS), is able to leverage Wikipedia's vast amount of knowledge and suggest a simple yet effective entity list for that article. To evaluate this, we utilized 1000 randomly selected English Wikipedia articles. The results showed that LENS successfully embeds the structured WKWD knowledge into the layered graph and offers clear improvements over baseline methods, utilizing Wikipedia's unique features to efficiently generate a simple yet effective entity list for that article.

The concept of ideal incompatible kidney transplants has been introduced to highlight the significant potential of crossmatching incompatible kidneys for improving waitlist patients' access to transplants. Currently, many such patients are at a high risk of not receiving a transplant before developing end-stage renal disease. To move forward, regulatory agencies and stakeholders must decide on establishing official standards for ideal incompatible kidneys. Doing so would provide the necessary foundation for funding, policy implementation, and public awareness campaigns. Ultimately, these efforts should result in more end-stage renal disease patients obtaining ideal incompatible kidney transplants from living donors, or deceased donors, thereby avoiding the negative impacts on living donors who may face financial difficulties due to the high cost of dialysis.

Recent advances in language understanding on tasks like machine translation and question answering have been made by training models on diverse datasets. The model's knowledge learned from these various datasets has been termed implicit connections, but this terminology is new and its implications are not yet fully understood. Our study delves into the nature of a model's implicit connections by utilizing frozen models to make several key observations. First, we find that the model's implicit connections enable it to generalize to unseen domains and facilitate it to perform well on related but unrelated questions. Second, we discover that some connections are erroneous and can be utilized to manipulate the model's output. Furthermore, we introduce three hypotheses to shed light on the nature of implicit connections. Additionally, we conduct an extensive visualization analysis to make the model's implicit connections more comprehensible and facilitate further research. All our evidence and resources, including connections across tasks, questions, and sentence segments, are made available on our website.

This paper delves into whether neural networks possess a true understanding of text, focusing on representing text semantics through numerical vectors. We scrutinize commonly accepted word vector theories by conducting experiments based on Loughran-McDonald's sentiment analysis dataset. Our findings suggest that while certain regression tasks can be performed with high accuracy, certain characteristics of the dataset might be influencing the results. Unfortunately, these results appear to not extend beyond sentiment analysis.

By utilizing multiple transmit antennas and a multiple-carrier modulation technique such as OFDM, we can significantly boost the efficiency of wireless systems that transfer both power and data simultaneously across wide areas. In our previous research, we developed and tested novel waveform designs using a single transmit antenna and a single receive antenna in an OFDM system that could achieve this additional gain. In this study, we extend our analysis to systems with multiple antennas by presenting a new equivalent model involving multiple antennas, a process that enables system optimization through established methods and leads to further novel solutions in the coming chapters.

A novel approach is presented to tackle complex phenomena during melting and freezing processes, such as phase boundary movement, latent heat release or absorption, and changes in material properties. The technique combines two methods: a level-set approach for simple situations and the embedded boundary technique for more intricate patterns. By representing the melting/freezing front as a single continuous shape, more basic topologies are achieved, which can be effectively handled using the level-set method. This technique has been integrated into a finite difference framework and will be demonstrated through both one-dimensional and two-dimensional benchmark problems, including the Voller--Krekelberg problem.

A quantum linguistic framework has been developed to model the non-associative nature of scalar quantity manipulation. This framework builds upon a quantum interpretation of the unary twist operator first suggested by Faralla and Cheng for natural language. The proposal extends this operator's application beyond binary combinations, allowing it to modulate quantities in isolation.

In multiplayer competitions, ensuring a rationally supportable equilibrium among participants can prove challenging. Our proposed solution addresses this by utilizing a learning algorithm capable of ensuring a rationalizable equilibrium as player participants make repeated decisions in a game. Essentially, the algorithm uses each player's past historical choices to make informed recommendations, eventually settling on strategies that support a rationalizable equilibrium. Notably, our algorithm requires only basic assumptions about the game, including no prior knowledge of the players' preferences. Furthermore, it has been proven that the time it takes to achieve a rationalizable equilibrium grows only linearly with the complexity of the game.

A Susceptible-Exposed-Infected-Recovered model is considered on a network, where an isolated node protects the network from an external infection and is removed if its protected status is compromised. A process occurs where infected nodes, adjacent to protected nodes, swap edges with randomly connected nodes, which are then incorporated into the infected network. The process of switching and the protection mechanism are analyzed in the context of preferential attachment networks. It is shown that protection against an external infection causes a phase transition, especially in relation to the ratio of nodes that rewire to the number of protected nodes. Interestingly, this ratio exhibits a critical value, beyond which the model exhibits exponential infection growth, reminiscent of a epidemic outbreak, while prior to this value, the infection spreads in a polynomial manner. Surprisingly, in certain regimes of the model with a high density of protected nodes and low rewiring rates, the model is capable of preventing the infection from spreading. It is also observed that this high-density regime is consistent with an undecayed preferential attachment network.

This research explores the interconnections between Cotton flow and both the structural and geometric properties of a nearly Kenmotsu 3-h-Manifold. Specifically, we identify conditions under which a manifold becomes invariant under the flow, and we establish that invariant manifolds will ultimately converge to a state of being Kenmotsu manifolds. Additionally, we establish necessary conditions for the existence of cotton solitons in relation to the 1-eigenspace of the tensor representing the manifold's geometry.

The framework combines numerical methods to update parton distribution functions, which are crucial for describing how partons are arranged within composite particles like protons. This affects the calculation of experimental cross-sections in hadronic processes. Given their fundamental role, Parton Distribution Functions are crucial in interpreting experimental data and are used extensively in particle physics experiments at facilities such as CLEO, BESSII, BESSIII, BESSIV, BESSV, BESSVI, BESSVII, BESSVIII, BESSIX, BESX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII, BESXVIII, BESXIX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII, BESXVIII, BESXIX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII, BESXVIII, BESXIX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII, BESXVIII, BESXIX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII, BESXVIII, BESXIX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII, BESXVIII, BESXIX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII, BESXVIII, BESXIX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII, BESXVIII, BESXIX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII, BESXVIII, BESXIX, BESXV, BESXVI, BESXVII

In reinforcement learning, accelerating policy convergence is a major focus of research. Specifically, combining value iteration with policy learning from environment samples is research that targets this goal. Though this approach usually yields positive outcomes when using supervised policy learning methods, the same approach when applied to value iteration leads to inconclusive results. This paper addresses this gap by introducing two innovative frameworks that integrate value iteration and policy learning from environment samples. First, we propose Infinite Experience Replay (IER) for value iteration, ensuring the solution matches Markov decision policy optimality. Second, we introduce the variance decrease replay (VDR) approach that reduces the variance of actions during policy optimization. Our results show both methods rapidly and accurately convert local samples into optimal policies. Experimental outcomes with state-of-the-art algorithms like C5 and PPO underline the effectiveness of the VDR approach in transforming IER's output into optimal policies within a limited experience in parallel environments.

We introduce libcommute, a reliable C++11 library that integrates with Python through pycommute. This integration allows sets of polynomial expressions (commuting or non-commuting) to be manipulated using the libcommute abstract operator and imported into Python using pycommute. We have employed libcommute to expand our own diagonalization framework, resulting in precise computations of eigenvalues and eigenvectors for large sparse matrices, with a potential scope of 10^7 by 10^7 matrices. Additionally, examples of its use include the exact computation of cluster sizes and gap distributions for the quantum Ising model, as well as the full spectrum of SU(3) cluster states under permutation and SU(3) matrix action.

Using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we analyzed the electronic structure of the bi-layer cuprate superconductor (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$, and found that its in-plane velocity was anomalously low, indicating the presence of an inauthentic electronic architecture, and an unexplained electronic void near the hole-like band was also observed, indicating a superconducting void. Comparing and analyzing our experimental and theoretical data revealed that an interfacial electron architecture and associated charge transfer could create this superconducting void. As a novel and unique interfacial phenomenon, this provides a pathway for manipulating such voids and paves the way for further theoretical and experimental investigations into multi-band superconductors, and raises questions about the potential for similar phenomena in other multi-band superconductors, and even those with single-band superconductivity.

A recent generalization of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation formula was analyzed, specifically for its application to the effective Lagrangian of QCD at high temperatures. We derived the transformation's conditions and a method to verify its correctness, then applied it to the Weyl fermion effective Lagrangian, resulting in an equivalent supersymmetric model. A comparison with the superbosonization approach yielded the same result for the supersymmetric gauge field. Additionally, we explored the superbosonization formalism's connection to the swampland criteria in high-temperature QCD.

The study of top quark spin offers significant insights and can aid in identifying new phenomena beyond the Standard Model. Despite their fleeting lifetimes, top quarks cannot decay hadronically without losing valuable information. Thus, decay leptons provide ideal final state signatures for investigation. In this paper, we examine various methods for estimating lepton polarization in single top quark production at the LHC, utilizing simulated data for the qT-channel process. Our analysis reveals that a neural network-based approach yields the most efficient outcome, capable of distinguishing between polarization and unpolarized components with a purity of 70%, surpassing traditional likelihood methods. This level of polarization estimation is achievable with the current LHC dataset and will further improve with increased data available in future runs. Consequently, such precision in determining polarization can significantly aid in identifying new heavy resonances decaying to electroweak boson and neutrino pairs.

Our research examines how modifications in laser writing impact the lattice structure and conductive properties of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ multilayered films.  We utilized ultrafast laser modifications to modify the films' conductive state.  Our observations through X-ray diffraction and Rutherford backscattering showed that the films maintain their cubic perovskite structure.  Our^8 Li $\beta$-observed NMR experiments revealed that the laser-written regions exhibit a highly metallic state with negligible resistance.  Our findings suggest that the metallic phase observed in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ interfaces may be the intrinsic nature of these materials, with our research providing valuable insights for improving their critical temperature.

In large-scale dialogue systems, the structure of conversation trees rapidly expands as the number of possible next steps increases at each frame. To effectively capture the high complexity and diversity of human conversations, we propose a new framework called MultiTalk, featuring a multi-to-multi branching mechanism. This innovative approach allows for simultaneous singular, multi-way, and bidirectional conversation options, providing greater flexibility in human interactions. We collected 4,739 human-human conversation datasets, spanning 1,059 separate conversation trees, and found that 61% of them contained elements of "back-channels" or "overlaps," and only 9% were effectively modeled by existing datasets. To address this gap, we created a novel dataset consisting of 3,415 multi-way conversation samples, and then conducted experiments showing that our proposed MultiTalk model outperforms existing alternatives in terms of generating accurate and high-quality conversation data.

This research investigates the potential of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) in wireless communications by examining an intelligent reflecting surface and multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system. We consider a scenario where both the MIMO transmitter and receiver experience correlated Rayleigh fading, and we aim to maximize the system's ergodic capacity under a total transmit power constraint. To address this challenge, we derive a closed-form expression for the system's ergodic capacity in two cases: when signal and interference phases are modeled as discrete random variables, and when they are represented as continuous variables. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of correlation and the number of intelligent reflecting surface and MIMO antennas on the system's ergodic capacity by providing closed-form expressions and insights into these parameters. Our results show that increasing the correlation coefficient, the number of transmitting antennas, or the number of intelligent reflecting surface and MIMO antennas can lead to an increase in the system's ergodic capacity.

We introduce a new class of alternative gravity theories known as conformal linking models, which are represented by a 2x2 matrix that connects two metrics. These theories are then analyzed in the context of cosmic evolution and the movement of particles, using a method called the Swiss-cheese approach. A specific type of simulation was performed to examine these theories during a merger of two galaxies, which revealed similarities to observations made with the Hubble Space Telescope. The results showed that the conformal linking models behave like $\Lambda$CDM in some aspects, which allowed for standard simulations to be used. Additionally, the models produced unique effects during the merger, which could potentially be detected by future detectors. The models are general enough to be applicable to a wide range of theories, which then provides a framework for scientists to study their theories during evolution and the movement of particles.

Recently, the driving functions for multiple stochastic Loewevitz (SLE) curves has been modeled through a discrete model known as the Zosnier-pan log-gas model, which incorporates the effects of Coulomb repulsion between the particles under an external potential, the study reveals the model's deep connection to the discrete Gaussian free field (GF$\grave{\textrm{e}}$e) in the context of Dirac boundary conditions. As the model undergoes a phase transition from a bounded to an unbounded configuration space, it displays characteristics similar to the ground state collapse seen in the Milne universe model. Furthermore, by analyzing the Gaussian component of the Gaussian mixture representation of the free field, a new multiple SLE model is derived where the curves interact through a repulsive force and are propelled by a $1/q$ strength, with this new model being bi-localized with the gas model for all parameters of interest. an intertwining relationship between the model and its "squared" counterpart is also discovered in the context of the Ding-Fedorov discrete GF$\grave{\textrm{e}}$e model which features free boundary conditions. this new insight leads to the derivation of the correlation functions for the M$_{2N}$ map of the discrete GF$\grave{\textrm{e}}$e model through the use of multiple sine functions with free boundary conditions.

MediaWiki-based systems are commonly used for collaborative document
creation, with Wikipedia being the most well-known example. WorkingWiki extends
this concept by incorporating a set of custom wiki pages that serve as a platform
for researchers to collaborate on both document generation and structured data.
These additional features include the ability to import cooperative datasets from
sources like JOGLDB, generate charts using D3, and seamlessly integrate with Overleaf
for real-time document co-editing. We have developed a generic extension for
any MediaWiki system, demonstrated its effectiveness with WorkingWiki, a collaborative
project aimed at producing an introductory guide to logic for both specialists and
non-specialists. WorkingWiki's development has been an iterative process, with our
research on user behaviors leading to an upgradable system that can enhance
any MediaWiki setup through its robust API.

To prevent the destructive effects of turbulent jet fires on offshore gas platforms, understanding how these fires interact with external influences is crucial. A better grasp of this interaction can be achieved through the development of advanced, real-time fire models that accurately account for external stimuli. This research aims to enhance current fire modeling techniques by creating a system that simulates the response of turbulent jet flames to sound waves. Using the concept of active flames and the AFSI active flame method, we successfully built a system capable of predicting the complex shapes of flames in 2D and 3D forms. By employing a Bayesian approach to linearize the flame structure, we were able to model the relationship between sound frequencies and flame shapes, providing a simplified, efficient representation of this interaction. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for integrating this modeling technique into broader, real-time fire simulation systems.

Stereoscopic measurements of stellar oscillation frequencies and stellar surface properties can be used to determine the internal structure and composition of stars through linear inverse theory. This approach yields a set of orthogonal functions known as modes, typically modes of the balance point (MODEB), where each mode has distinct physical characteristics. However, standard perturbation theories result in generic, non-geometric mode representations. Machine learning techniques have produced a different type of mode set, where each mode exhibits specific geometric and physical properties, but these modes lack the orthogonality required for accurate structural insights. This paper delves into the characteristics of the geometric mode set and compares it to the MODEB mode set, highlighting the trade-offs between surface geometry and internal star information, as well as the evolution of stellar modes during different stages of development.

Time series analysis offers a straightforward and computationally efficient way to classify complex dynamics in networks of interacting neurons. In this study, we develop a universal algorithm based on shape similarity to identify multiple dynamics, including the recently discovered chimera states, in networks. Our method outlines the entire distribution of dynamics by extracting typical temporal patterns and comparing them with a reference pattern, thus providing a complete and transparent view of network activity. Our findings show that this algorithm produces accurate results even when applied to real-world data and is unaffected by the use of invasive filtering techniques like thresholding. Furthermore, the robustness of this universal detector outperforms other prominent methods in detecting and distinguishing multiple dynamics in traveling wave and synchronization scenarios. Our method also surpasses the widely used coexistence index in detecting traveling chimeras in coupled phase oscillators. Consequently, this method can serve as the foundation for designing resilient machine learning techniques to identify and classify the elusive traveling chimeras in networks of spiking neurons.

A detailed examination of two-dimensional, site-based random Ising models has been
conducted with 'nearest neighbor' interactions included. Given that these additional
interactions lead to 'cluster' behavior at low temperatures, characteristics of these
clusters were analyzed as a function of temperature and the model's p-spin parameter.
Since these parameters influence the model's long-term, high-temperature response, a
significant observation emerged: above the initial transition temperature, some large
cluster characteristics abruptly plummet. These characteristics match those of the
model's primary ordering phenomenon. The interplay between these matching features and
model theoretical variants was also explored.

We investigate the impact of a possible interaction between neutrinos and an ultralight dark substance on the neutrinoless double beta decay spectrum and the decay rates of dense astrophysical objects like neutron stars and supernovae. If the mass of the light dark substance is much greater than the neutrino mass, a distinct peak appears in the decay spectrum, corresponding to a dark matter particle plus neutron pair produced from neutrino decay. However, this peak would have not been observed in the Neutrina experiment data. Moreover, limits on the neutrino-dark matter interaction derived from neutron star and supernova cooling processes are significantly tighter than those from lab experiments for interaction strengths that lead to rapid neutron star cooling.

To address the issue of solar ultraviolet interference in astronomical observations using solar array telescopes and photon detectors sensitive to the L1 to L3 wavelength range due to the scattering of ultra-high energy solar photons by the solar magnetic field, the flux of such photons was simulated under the influence of the solar magnetic field. This simulation incorporated blackbody radiation from the solar surface, tracking the evolution of electron and proton energies, and the resulting polarization of the radiated sunlight, considering the strong solar surface magnetic field. The calculated ultra-high energy photon flux exceeded the flux of original solar radiation by over three to four orders of magnitude at typical solar frequencies when electrons and protons reached equilibrium, potentially exceeding the supply of low-energy photons necessary to prevent solar surface evaporation and even leading to its collapse. Furthermore, the simulated flux of ultra-high energy photons, taking into account their spatial distribution and polarization, was found to be comparable to observed fluxes of meteors during solar space probe passes, although the expected flux at the Earth's surface was significantly lower than the normal cosmic ray flux at the Earth's surface. Additionally, solar observations using large solar arrays and highly sensitive optical detectors at L1 to L3 frequencies may actually detect the expected ultra-high energy meteor-like flux.

In the nonlocal gravitation model proposed within general relativity, a simplified approach is taken to derive a set of four vector fields, known as tetrads, from a more abstract, nonlocal connection in a flat spacetime. The study focuses on identifying the minimum requirements for the connection to ensure the resulting tetrads satisfy specific mathematical properties required for a coherent gravitational theory. The study also explores various scenarios where the connection can be reformulated in terms of physical quantities measurable within general relativity, including a situation where the connection reflects a form of modified gravity called Galileon.

Conflicting writes to a shared document from multiple users are a significant issue that must be addressed in Conflict-free Replicated Data Forms (CRDFs). To resolve this problem, a system must either eliminate conflicting transactions or modify the data to resolve conflicts. Traditionally, CRDFs have focused heavily on consistency but at the expense of performance, neglecting other crucial system properties. We argue that consistency should be just one aspect of a multi-objective design approach. To move away from consistency-centric designs, we introduce a new ERDF design that treats conflicts as redundant information. Our proposed framework prioritizes eliminating conflicting writes to maintain data clarity. Specifically, we outline a system with features including a high-performance index, conflict detection using a bitmap, and a conflict-resolution mechanism with a Conflict Eradication-Win (CEW) strategy. By adopting CEW, the system achieves stronger data transparency and relevance without compromising on the advantages of data clarity. We validate the effectiveness of CEW through the implementation of a prototype, demonstrating its potential as a viable solution for conflict management in CRDFs.

Our analysis of genomic data integrated functional information from 1000 Genomes Project with association studies across 18 human traits identified significant disparities in allele frequency between genomic regions. Regions of active transcription exhibited a notable increase in both taggable alleles and missing heritability when compared to inactive regions. This pattern held consistent across multiple species and was particularly evident in highly functional regions, which exhibited allele frequency similarities across humans and mice. Furthermore, we discovered an excess of taggable alleles in regions linked to neurodevelopmental disorders and human height, and low-fraction regions showed greater allele frequency differentiation between humans and chimpanzees, indicating potentially higher complexity in these areas. Conversely, genetic variation in regions associated with immune system function and metabolic processes showed greater differentiation when examined. Lastly, we observed a distinct allele frequency pattern in regions linked to gene copy number variations, where variation in these regions had little impact on protein sequence but altered gene expression levels. Our comprehensive examination of nucleotide functionality reveals nuanced insights into the distribution of genetic variation and its impact on human traits beyond binary measures of active or inactive genomic regions.

Proton-proton collisions at the LHC enable the study of rare phenomena resulting from heavy scalar or vector bosons with unusually large masses. These particles, such as Higgs or $Z$ bosons, may not be producible via standard processes and instead need to be created initially in a heavy macro-object, termed as "tiny systems". Considering the production of an extra quark-flavour, we compare inclusive and semi-inclusive processes, noting that the latter, where an additional charged hadron is included, offer enhanced significance. By utilizing differential measurements, specifically, we demonstrate a notable improvement, nearly 20%, in sensitivity, with the gain rising for smaller $\beta$ values in a dictation from jet $p_{\mathrm{T}}$. Furthermore, increasing luminosity in ATLAS and upgrading the collider to LHCq, with its potential for producing "tiny systems" via quantum electroweak interactions, may provide insights into quark flavour production, potentially exceeding current capabilities, which are limited by systematic uncertainties. Ultimately, we emphasize the significance of theoretical and experimental efforts to refine the "tiny systems" framework, with simulations indicating a substantial portion of Higgs production via associated heavy quarks, approximately 60%, occurring in such "tiny systems".

Analysis of 19 inactive X-ray sources in the central region of the Milky Way was conducted, using 10 years of data from the XMM-Newton and Chandra telescopes, to understand the repetition intervals of neutron star binaries in a quiet state. A key feature of this population is the strong correlation discovered between the repetition intervals and the rates at which the stars accrete material. This relationship is distinct from one previously found in the overall population of quiet X-bins, likely due to differences in the populations of these sources. The origin of this separate population could be due to a difference in the nature of the binary systems, a lack of observation of short-period systems in this region of the galaxy, or the presence of a population of inactive low-mass X-ray binaries with a repetition period of one year or less. This last possibility is constrained to less than 10 percent of this quiet population. Additionally, a separate population of inactive X-bins with a repetition interval of one year or less may be partially hidden in some features of the quiet soft gamma repeater and magnetized population. The relationship between the repetition intervals of these sources and a previously reported correlation between their repetition periods and separation distances could provide insight into the population of this quiet X-bin population in the central region of the galaxy. A key constraint discovered in this analysis was that there are likely more than 10 inactive X-bins with a repetition interval of 10 years or less in the central region of

The binary test of gravity, a highly productive area of research over the last half-century, has significant limitations due to the scarcity of available data and reliance on limited sources, mainly pulsars influenced by strong general relativity. In contrast, radio astrometry from high-precision sub-milliarcsecond levels allows extensive binary tests of gravity in major systems, including the Sun-Earth, Sun-Venus, and Mars orbits. These tests pass all general relativity predictions with notable margins, often exceeding a factor of 100. Further, the outcome strongly suggests that the gravitational constant remains constant on a scale of at least $10^{-11}$ per year.

Using the Stacking technique, we analyzed the radio properties of compact faint (CF) radio sources at 1.4 GHz by combining the depth of the APOGEE survey with the sensitivity of the APOGPQ and APOGEE-N spectra. Our stack spectra exhibit a flat spectrum characteristic, which is a hallmark of radio galaxies. Further analysis revealed that compact faint (CF) sources have no evident relationship between their flux density and spectral index when considering a wide frequency range. However, at narrower bandwidths, particularly between $W_{500}$ and $W_{2000}$, a negative correlation was found. The correlation disappears when considering wider bandwidths. Also, our analysis did not show any evident correlation with source morphological features. CF sources do not exhibit significant relationships with their angular diameter, ellipticity, or asymmetry. The results of our analysis are comparable to previous ones. Furthermore, our additional parameter does not show any evident correlation, which is distinct from our prior findings.

A numerical simulation framework is developed to model how hydrodynamic waves traveling through gaseous envelopes of stars interact with the boundaries, as seen in scenarios like exoplanet atmospheric studies and stellar eruptions. When significant energy is transferred by these waves, they can generate shocks that may spread across the star's surface. Using specialized hydrodynamic solvers, we examine the envelope's heating caused by these shocks and their impact on embedded objects. An example is created by inflating a spherical shell of gas, then introducing a sudden shock. It is found that low-frequency waves below 0.1 erds (where an earth is one oscillation period) generally do not create global shocks, but higher-frequency waves can produce a coherent shock front. This occurs due to nonlinear wave-Envelope interactions. Despite this, good agreement with theoretical predictions is achieved by using an effective viscosity model that accounts for turbulent mixing of the envelope's envelope. This allows us to efficiently simulate MHD stellar eruptions while capturing important effects of these interactions.

This research explores modularity lifting theorems for Galois representations,
focusing on both arithmetic and non-arithmetic cases. A key contribution is a new
modularity lifting theorem applicable to general weights, whether arithmetic or
non-arithmetic. Additionally, we establish a critical surjectivity condition for
non-arithmetic weights. As an application, this condition allows us to lift a class
of representations to a wide range of non-arithmetic weights.

Molecular oscillations significantly impact electronic properties and should ideally be considered in theoretical calculations of electron-related phenomena. Typically, the effects of spin and electron-vibration interactions are analyzed using a Schrodinger equation, which doesn't account for momentum. However, the Schrodinger equation is merely a special case of the more comprehensive Hohenberg-Mermin equation, which does include momentum. By formulating a general framework based on the Hohenberg-Mermin equation, an abstract representation of electron-vibration interactions was created, applicable to any type of momentum-dependent system. For the specific case of semiconductor crystals, a more detailed model was derived, in which Schrodinger-based electron-vibration interactions are combined with a realistic description of the impact of phonons (sound waves) on the overall system. This formulation was then used to derive a non-zero value for the electron-vibration coupling matrix element, in contrast to the conventional view which suggests that this value should be zero. As a result, it is demonstrated that molecular vibrations induce a measurable electron-vibration coupling effect that influences emission or absorption of electrons and vibrational energy, in contrast to the standard view which suggests that these effects should be zero due to energy and momentum conservation principles. Furthermore, our electron-vibration coupling scheme can be applied to any type of momentum-dependent system, in which Schrodinger-based electron-vibration interactions that don't arise from molecular bonds become relevant, in contrast to the conventional theory which suggests that these effects should be zero

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an accessible introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack of comprehensive overview papers on the topic.

The use of named entities and numbers has consistently been a difficult aspect for both humans and machines to fully comprehend due to the multiple meanings they can have. This study aims to explore how both humans and machines handle semantic variety in written text when making inferences using natural language. Both competitive and cooperative contexts were examined in this study. Through forced choice tasks, natural language inference models and people were presented with pairs of interpretations for entities and numbers within written sentences. The data collected from people showed that prior meanings of entities and numbers, as well as their competition or cooperation, have a lasting effect on interpreting written sentences. The performance of machines was then compared to human results with mixed outcomes. Notably, current natural language inference systems outperform people in some aspects related to numbers but consistently fail to match human performance on written tokens of entities. These findings highlight areas for improvement in both the training data and models of natural language inference systems. Furthermore, the study provides valuable insights into how machines process and apply prior knowledge in both competitive and cooperative settings.

When changing lanes, drivers must assess their surroundings carefully to avoid accidents.  Using deep learning, we built a system that classifies video clips of drivers as either safe or dangerous when they change lanes. First, we segmented objects in the video clips with a semantic mask transfer method. Then, we fed the resulting masked video clips into a temporal classification model. This approach gave us higher accuracy than an alternative where we classified the clips without segmentation. The mask transfer method let us use video clips recorded on real cars, making our system more applicable in practice.

The potential for young brown dwarfs and giant planets to reach mass-shedding rotational thresholds has been explored through hydrodynamical simulations. By adding lateral rotation to gravitational and thermal forces in 3D simulations, the mass-shedding limits for rotating low-mass stars, brown dwarfs, and the smallest gas giants were calculated over a wide range of ages. Key factors were analyzed to observe how they evolve in rotating objects up to their mass-shedding limits, comparing them to non-rotating counterparts. Results revealed that in rapidly spinning brown dwarfs and gas giants, material along the equator tends to be expelled, whereas in rotating young gas giants, central contraction can counterbalance expansion due to rotation in the outer layers.

As the luminosity of the Large Hadron Collider increases, precise measurements of scattering processes are becoming more accurate, potentially revealing new effects beyond the standard model when combined with accurate theoretical calculations. Such measurements often involve highly complex objects, making it challenging to model their interactions using conventional methods. A novel numerical approach resolves this issue by transforming the data into a form that can be directly utilized in amplitude calculations, maintaining high precision and efficiency. This method effectively captures the characteristics of heavily jet-like structures formed in energy-colliding particle interactions.

A new dynamic model has been created to explain the diverse observed characteristics of afterglows associated with gamma-ray bursts, taking into consideration the influence of the interstellar medium on the observed radiative outcomes. The model introduces a dimensional parameter that allows it to adapt to the extensive observed range of afterglow behavior, and as this parameter takes on specific values, the model can be connected to the well-established theoretical fireball models. Furthermore, given the limited data available from metal-poor environments, the model makes new predictions about the future observation of gamma-ray bursts and their associated afterglows in such environments.

A bipartite vertex division of a graph $G$ occurs when its vertices are partitioned into three sets, $A$, $B$, and $C$, such that each edge of $G$ belongs to a specific pair of these sets. We've developed a novel approach for verifying bipartite vertex divisions, allowing us to confirm if a given graph has such a division of depth $k$ in time proportional to $2^{O(k^2)}$ times the number of vertices. As a result, we can also efficiently identify the smallest set of vertices, in polynomial time, to make a graph bipartite division-friendly.

Deep neural network-based recognition systems have generally achieved high accuracy, yet their performance diminishes significantly when trained on balanced datasets. Moreover, most practical applications require the system to learn from new, unlabeled data in the future, which constitutes the challenge of incremental learning. Researchers have developed various incremental learning approaches, but they often fail when combined with unbalanced datasets due to the issue of catastrophic interference, where the system forgets previous data when learning from new data. In our study, we examine the incremental learning from balanced datasets scenario, acknowledging that while learning environments may be unbalanced, the data for each new class learned is typically uniform and balanced. To validate our assumption, we collected and annotated a diverse set of datasets covering multiple types of objects and actions. To effectively train models in this type of learning setting, we propose eight strategies to calibrate model outputs, ensuring they output balanced probabilities. To assess their efficacy, we calibrated eight popular incremental learning models, evaluating them on the proposed data settings using both synthetic and real-world datasets. To ensure a statistically significant result, we conducted additional experiments through pairwise comparisons. Our calibrated models demonstrate substantial improvements in both accuracy and low bias errors, outperforming their uncalibrated counterparts by up to 20% in accuracy and 40% in low bias errors, while also providing calibrated output scores that better reflect the true distribution.
