Traditional bipedal locomotion designs focus on balancing stability and energy efficiency, typically assuming well-known environmental conditions and neglecting the influence of wind resistance. Although the ассистенция propulsion can enhance energy performance by up to two orders of magnitude on mild winds, its impact on resilience is rarely investigated. In this study, we introduce the first bilateral propulsion-assisted locomotion system, and optimize itsAssistence to minimize energy consumption while ensuring maximum resilience. Our results reveal that propulsion-assisted movement leads to significant energy savings, and allows for larger perturbation recovery ranges by at least one and a half times compared to unassisted movement. Furthermore, our optimal strategy ensures the preservation of propulsion benefits and robust perturbation recovery capabilities. In contrast to prior approaches, which typically assume constant velocities, our design enables varying speed profiles. We also examine the effects of different propulsionAssistенция levels and compare our method to commonly used control systems.

A respected field $F$ of characteristic $p > 0$ and complete valuation $v$ comes with an associated residue field $k = k_v$. We are interested in the ability of a polynomial $f \in k[T_1, \dots, T_d]$ to uniquely associate each element of $k^d$ with a unique root, which we term a complete residue system or CRS-mapping property. It was previously established by multiple researchers that such a polynomial exists if the valuation ring $\mathcal{O}_v$ contains specific elements $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_d$ that satisfy certain conditions and can be transformed into a unique set of roots by a polynomial $f$ which reduces to the given polynomial $f$ in the residue field. However, the existing proofs are limited to cases where the residue field $k$ is a finite field. In this paper, which extends the results of existing research, it is shown that the valuation ring $\mathcal{O}_v$ does contain such an element $\alpha = (\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_d)$ for any valuation $v$ with a complete valuation ring, which implies the existence of a polynomial $f$ which maps each element of $k^d$ to a unique root, even when the residue field $k$ is an infinite field.

Modern high-performance processors, despite their impressive capabilities, suffer from underutilization due to energy and performance constraints. To address this issue, Arch-based Underutilized Rate Effective Processor Design (AUREP) is introduced, which focuses on enhancing CPU efficiency by optimizing system effectiveness rather than peak performance. By analyzing three crucial aspects of system efficiency, namely supply, demand, and rate, AUREP identifies the most critical performance bottlenecks through the concept of Hyper-blocks. As a design guideline, AUREP recommends prioritizing optimizations that reduce activity at the memory level. Applying these principles to two baseline systems results in the development of two innovative CPU architectures, namely HyperReduce and HyperSource, featuring innovative techniques such as HyperDegrade, HyperSourceReduce, and others. When compared to state-of-the-art commercial processors, the proposed designs exhibit superior efficiency across a wide range of system benchmarks, exhibiting up to 27% greater rate efficiency and 2.7x greater memory-level reduction. Notably, the innovative approaches introduced, such as micro-op caching and multi-functional pipelines, have significant potential for direct implementation in commercial processors.

To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the anomalous magnetic dipole moment of a muon, the relevant contribution needs to be at least of the same order as the difference, which is approximately 7 sigma. However, the direct contribution from the Higgs to this magnetic moment is many additional orders of magnitude smaller. In addition, topquark loops contribute very little to the topquark loop contributions can vary by nearly two orders of magnitude due to the unknown value of the Yukawa coupling. Despite this, the topquark loop contributions can vary significantly due to the unknown value of the Yukawa coupling. As a result, the contribution from the Higgs sector cannot sufficiently explain the anomaly in the magnetic dipole moment of the muon within the Standard Model.

Using tree-level decays such as $B_c^+\to \mu^+ \overline{\nu}_\mu \, \gamma$, 
$\tau^+ \to \mu^+ \, \overline{\nu}_\tau \, \gamma$, and $D_s^+\to \mu^+ \, \overline{\nu}_\mu \, \gamma$, 
we establish the most precise yet unconstrained world averages for the universal 
coupling $\gamma$ in the Standard Model. 
By combining these decay rates, we derive $\gamma$ at the highest level of precision 
to date. 
Additionally, incorporating theoretical predictions helps us understand the 
importance of radiative and long-distance contributions, which may be explored 
experimentally with high-luminosity data.

A knot is a prime traditional link when it's a prime link that's not a Hopf link,
and many questions about traditional knots can also be asked of link types.
Knots differ from welded knots in the inversion rule at crossings and superpositions.
We present a new move to untie a welded or traditional knot, and provide the
unknotting conditions for the (8,3) torus knot under this rule. We also explore
how this move and the given example affect the fundamental group representation
of knots, as well as the application of the Doi-Hokomaev invariant in predicting
unknotting results.

A key result in algebraic geometry is the theorem of Gromov-Stierman which shows the rationality of a smooth curve's Jacobian when its genus is at least two. Using novel techniques from tropical geometry, we've found a finite set of equations that fully describe the semigroup of a curve's divisor in relation to its genus. This description relates to the curve's Jacobian through the semigroup's set generators, a feature of interest in both tropical and algebraic geometry.

We demonstrate that both the length and complexity of a Vassiliev characteristic of order three derived from the fundamental 2-loop structure behave as optimal. Furthermore, we establish that this specific configuration yields a non-trivial indicator for the third Vassiliev invariant.

We also provide a concrete method to determine whether a given closed loop can be classified as a knot or merely forms a topological structure without knotting, by calculating a specific value based on the second loop's distance in a particular geometric measurement. If this calculated value does not equal zero, the closed loop is guaranteed to exhibit knotting properties.

We demonstrate that this method produces an efficient calculation whose underlying complexity increases at most at the rate of the square root of the number of components in the input, thus proving it to be an effective indicator. Additionally, we discuss how this approach relates to previous topological characterization methods but outperforms them in terms of computational efficiency.

New research by the KATRIN collaboration supports earlier findings suggesting an upper limit for neutrino mass, yet introduces a new approach to establish a lower limit. By analyzing specific situations and applying energy conservation principles, a lower limit for neutrino mass can be determined through precise measurements of certain variables, including the electron rest mass. This research demonstrates that the determined lower limit for neutrino mass is at least 0.045 times the universal constant divided by the speed of the electrons.

As operações de matriz são intensivas em cálculos e memória, o que as torna adequadas para testes comparativos entre processamento sequencial e paralelo. No caso sequencial, foi utilizado um algoritmo de Bloch com um processador Intel Core i5, enquanto para o processamento paralelo, foi utilizado o OpenMP com uma placa de vídeo NVIDIA GeForce GT 710. Os resultados mostram que, embora a abordagem paralela seja teoricamente mais eficiente, o algoritmo de Bloch supera o método clássico de Gauss-Jordan para tamanhos de matriz acima de 50x50. Já a abordagem baseada em shaders demonstra ser eficaz para matrizes maiores a partir de 100x100.

Our proposed method enables a team of mobile agents to effectively cooperate in a range of missions, such as surveillance and target engagement, by working together through conventional communication systems. The agents are limited in their ability to process information and communicate, which necessitates a collaborative approach that involves making decisions within the context of constrained resources. Our method utilizes a pre-established graph to represent the agents' relationships and then applies a tactical collaboration operator to adjust the graph based on the agents' computations and communications. This adjustment ensures that the team maintains effective coordination and continues to collaborate efficiently. Furthermore, our method ensures that the agents' actions converge to an optimal solution, as demonstrated by theoretical proof. These features provide our method with the ability to adapt to changing missions and environments, as well as the ability to learn from failed attempts.

Quantum corrections to scattering processes at high energies or many loops tend to alter the leading behavior of tree-level processes, potentially undermining the validity of perturbation theory. To rectify this, all relevant quantum corrections must be systematically incorporated within the effective action governing the physical processes. As a result, slight modifications are necessary within the classical field configuration, thereby preserving the accuracy of the amplitude at tree-level when combined with large corrections. Our initial findings involve demonstrating how these corrections to the classical field configuration depend on both position and momentum, solving a long-standing ambiguity in this dependence. Moreover, we discover that corrections contain a novel type of pole, which carries essential information about the system. We also investigate a theoretical connection between this configuration and supersymmetric theories, in the context of N=4 theory and multi-gluon scattering at next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order.

With the rapid expansion of educational institutions across nations, advanced technology has been integrated into learning spaces to enhance teaching and learning processes. Though these tech tools bring significant benefits, they also pose security risks, particularly in matters of student privacy. While existing research focuses on protective measures, returning educational data to its original owner without revealing any other information to potential assaulters is also possible. This concept is referred to as a pragmatic privacy assault, and in this study, we introduce a method called VPE-Net to allow an attacker to recover educational information from multiple institutions in a vertical setup. VPE-Net utilizes a minimal amount of additional data, or side information, possessed by the attacker to further improve the assault's effectiveness. Our study demonstrates the need for focusing on the protectiveness of sharing educational data with external parties, in addition to shielding it from unauthorized access within the institution. Moreover, researchers should also investigate the limitations of defensive techniques in preventing such data protection breaches.

Nonparametric density estimation is commonly performed using kernel density estimation, which has been proven to be an effective and versatile tool. Building upon this, we develop a novel approach that utilizes a set of precomputed Fourier attributes to estimate density functions. Our method involves transforming data into a form that reveals underlying patterns, from which we derive a kernel estimator. We prove that this estimator converges to the true underlying density function, and through numerical experiments, we demonstrate its performance under various scenarios.

In our previous research, we established that the symmetric group $S_n$ cannot be embedded into any Cartesian product of trees, building on a result by Alon and Tardos which showed the same for $S_{10}$. In this study, we expand upon these findings by proving the cannot-embed status for groups $G$ whose order is at least half of $|G|$ in any Garland product of trees, thereby extending the result of Alon and Tardos. Our main approach involves a new Cartesian technique and an innovative strategy known as the Cartesian Decomposition Method. This method enables us to apply Alon and Tardos's method of replacing elements with groups to obtain the results: (1) $S_{10}$ cannot be embedded into any Garland product of trees per our prior findings, and (2) $S_{10}$ cannot be embedded into any Garland product of trees, and (3) $B_6$ cannot be embedded into any Garland product of tuples of trees, and (4) $B_6 \times S_3$ cannot be embedded into any Garland product of tuples of trees.

This research examines a conformally invariant mathematical structure known as the M\"obius structure on a compact hypersurface in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$, developing the foundational theory of M\"obius scalar curvature and demonstrating its robustness under small perturbations of the M\"obius curvature function $\mathcal{H}$. Specifically, it is established that the M\"obius scalar curvature $\mathcal{R}$ attains a local minimum under the transformation of a hypersurface $f$ along a conformal vector field $\xi$ in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ when the M\"obius second fundamental form satisfies the semi-parallel condition with respect to its associated connection and the M\"obius structure on $f$ satisfies specific divergence requirements. Furthermore, multiple geometrically meaningful sufficient conditions for the M\"obius structure to satisfy these complex conditions are provided, including a case where the M\"obius structure on $f$ exhibits constant M\"obius scalar curvature.

Automated cardiac magnetic resonance (MRI) image analysis relies heavily on accurate anatomical information. MRI technology uses non-invasive imaging to visualize internal body structures. A specific type of heart defect, congenital heart disease, affects approximately 0.6 per thousand live births and includes a wide range of abnormalities. MRI scans are the gold standard for diagnosing and monitoring these defects. However, different types of abnormalities can make MRI analysis challenging due to altered cardiac anatomy. We investigated the level of accuracy with which existing cardiac segmentation models can identify structures in patients with rare congenital heart defects. Using two established segmentation frameworks, we evaluated seven cases with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and two cases with single ventricle physiology. We discovered that models produced highly precise results for areas of interest in defect patients, with mean distances of 1.23 and 1.24 millimeters, respectively. However, they also exhibited excessive smoothing in some regions, potentially missing critical details. In contrast, models for defect patients performed less accurately on MRI images with normal hearts, with an increase in mean distance of 0.5 millimeters. These findings highlight the limitations with which current cardiac segmentation models can be applied to patients with rare congenital heart defects for surgical planning. In conclusion, while existing models demonstrate a high level of accuracy with this patient population, they also exhibit reduced performance with MRI images with normal hearts, indicating a level of sensitivity to certain anatomical variations.

This study summarizes recent advancements in gradient fracture theories across various classes of materials, including hyperelastic, viscoelastic, and nonlinear dissipative materials. Existing research has already established a common framework in elastic and fracture mechanics, and our work expands on this by exploring how gradient models can be applied to a broader range of materials while maintaining a unified understanding. Furthermore, we delve into open questions within the field of calculus of variations, addressing both finite and infinite domain problems.

A novel SWIPT-enabled wireless system, comprising an access point that transmits data and energy to a set of wireless terminals, was investigated in this study. To maximize overall efficiency, a multi-objective optimization problem was formulated which balances the terminals' data transmission efficiency and energy conversion efficiency. The problem was initially reformed as a quadratic programming issue, before being solved using Lagrangian relaxation. A subsequent iterative algorithm using a penalty function was developed to solve the original problem. Further, a new iterative algorithm based on convex optimization was proposed. The validity of these algorithms was verified through simulation results, demonstrating the benefits of prioritizing different wireless services through adjustable parameters.

Recommender systems are typically categorized as trust-based if they rely on user opinions from past purchases, or as search systems otherwise, given their inherent social nature. Previous research into these platforms has been conducted under the assumption that users provide flawless reviews. However, the quality of reviews may be compromised by the influence of product company advertising. Consequently, past studies have examined various aspects of user behavior and data, assuming search platforms without the consideration of their social nature or user-generated content's variability. To bridge these concepts, the present paper proposes the RIAS dataset, which captures both aspects of user behavior and data, offering additional value for the community.

Complex systems, whether found in nature or created by humans, are often studied by focusing on specific conditions that can reveal their outer limits. To understand these systems more effectively, researchers are increasingly using extreme conditional modeling, which aims to capture the inherent connections between rare events. This approach has been applied in fields such as weather forecasting, where the link between heatwaves and heavy rainfall is an example of dependent extremal behavior. In this context, a method based on block maxima and conditional tail independence is used to develop a model that can handle such situations. Furthermore, a simulation demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in estimating a conditionally extreme quantile function.

Recent advancements in automated thesauri have been made using sense disambiguation of technical terms based on their context, however, general-purpose model performance in this area is relatively limited. To overcome this limitation, the success of pre-trained language models is being leveraged through specialized model construction that incorporates both textual and phonetic information to create a multi-dimensional embedding space. A new model, called GlossBERT, is constructed by integrating morpho-semantic information from a Chinese term's pinyin and its Hans dictionary definitions, resulting in significantly improved sense disambiguation performance, outperforming a traditionally widely used baseline model by a significant margin.

A significant portion of the world's population lacks access to essential skills needed for self-sufficiency and employability. Technical instructions, when made available visually in a language-comprehensible format, can bridge this gap by enabling individuals to acquire new skills from various disciplines, including complex tasks like using machinery. However, the current state of multimodal instructional content is inconsistent in quality, as the relationship between visual examples and written text can vary from useful to confusing. The primary objective of this research is to establish key features that high-quality multimodal instructional content must possess by examining how professionals use such content to execute tasks. The data collected from expert observations, when subjected to a process modeling technique, reveals four essential characteristics of effective multimodal instructional content: (1) clarity in the sequence of actions depicted in visual examples and written text, (2) seamless integration of visual examples and written text, (3) minimal reliance on external knowledge, and (4) universal applicability. The proposed design principles can serve as a foundation for the creation of high-quality multimodal instructional content, with potential applications in addressing the global lack of access to essential skills.

The exponential growth of vertices in a graph like the Cayley graph of a group can be contrasted with the relatively slow, polynomial growth of normal subgroups. To bridge this discrepancy, we investigate an intermediate range, or 'avalanche zone,' between these two extremes. Through the use of random walk techniques and the application of free differential calculus, we establish the distribution of this intermediate zone. Specifically, we determine the probability of finding an avalanche of a certain size, a result that is consistent with the normal subgroup and polynomial growth regimes, as well as various intermediate cases.

In this study, we derive an explicit formula for a wide range of moments in the universal Airy polynomial family, which includes the standard Airy polynomials as a particular case. For orthogonal polynomials, a similar strategy has been employed in the research by Bousseau and Rouault (2019). Furthermore, our statistical ensembles can be understood as modifications of the standard Gaussian unitary ensemble, which has been confirmed through the application of the 'method of deformed ensembles', introducing new deforming parameters. These additional parameters introduce varying behaviors in the large-$N$ limit, leading to different phase transitions. These changes can be effectively modeled using the resolvent's Riemann surface, which features multiple sheets connected by branching cuts. The positions of these cuts are effectively determined by the equilibrium measure of two interacting systems of particles, which consists of multiple components and whose boundary conditions are set by the varying parameters of the matrix model. The effective potential of this system can be successfully analyzed using the method of 'semiclassical limits', which involves the application of 'periodic Schr\"odinger operators' with specific boundary conditions on their periodic domains.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors is limited by the angle at which the laser enters the detector's recycling system. A more precise laser alignment could significantly release existing capacity in the detection system's bandwidth. A novel angle-Sagnac interferometer design has been proposed to replace the traditional recycling system, offering enhanced high-frequency sensitivity through a symbolic transformation of the detection system's mathematics. This research explores the performance potential of this innovative design through simulation and found that the angle-Sagnac design exhibits superior high-frequency responsiveness compared to the conventional system at equal power levels. The study also found that the novel design could retain the superior performance characteristics of a previous sloshing interferometer design.

In high-frequency communications, multiple antenna systems are prevalent, and their performance heavily relies on accurate visibility data. However, traditional methods for obtaining visibility data assume that interference can be effectively separated, which isn't always feasible given the large number of antennas used. Assuming a certain level of unmodeled noise, we investigate the probability that a certain amount of unmodeled noise results in some antennas remaining isolated from their corresponding devices within an existing large-scale MIMO wireless system, utilizing a stochastic access protocol. We derive a precise mathematical expression for this probability, and a simplified form for practical use, and our findings are supported by simulations. Furthermore, we explore how certain system parameters influence this probability in the context of MIMO systems with hundreds or even thousands of antennas.

Building on previous research, our study examines how protoplanetary disks might develop bumpy structures due to vertical shear instability (VSI). In Part 1, we found that VSI could result in non-axisymmetric density waves at various spatial scales, potentially creating substructures. To move forward, we used radiative transfer in 2D to determine how these substructures influence the disk's dust emission. Our results showed that VSI-driven interactions between gas and dust could generate non-axisymmetric dust features that could be detected with high-resolution next-generation telescopes like JWARS and VLT/ESPRESSO. The formation of these dust structures would be a signature of VSI, and their patterns and shapes could provide insights into the underlying physics of the disk. Furthermore, our research implies that VSI might influence the distribution of carbon monoxide and water molecules in the disk, and that these structures could be observed using spectroscopic techniques. Carbon monoxide formations would be trapped in VSI structures at specific distances from the central star, and water formations could create non-axisymmetric substructures in both the inner and outer regions of the disk. In summary, our modeling results suggest that VSI could create observable dust and molecular structures in protoplanetary disks, and these structures have the potential to be detected with advanced telescopes and provide insights into the disk's formation process.

To model the shape of the earth, scientists use a geoid model to account for variations in gravity across different locations. A similar concept, often referred to as the "big apple" effect, applies to atomic nuclei, where surface gravity varies significantly depending on the distribution of mass within the nucleus. Research into this phenomenon has been conducted both theoretically and experimentally. In a geoid, this variation is observed as approximately 0.5%, whereas in nuclei, the difference in "gravity" can exceed 500 keV. Calculating the form factor of nuclei requires a precise model of this "big apple" effect. Similarly, the astrophysical application of this phenomenon is seen in neutron stars, where gravity variations surpass 10%. To address this, a relativistic density functional approach has been developed, allowing for a consistent treatment of this effect. The accuracy of this model has been validated against experimental data, including electron scattering and muonic hydrogen absorption. A future experiment at the CERN facility is proposed to further explore this phenomenon.

Using experimental data for optical losses, we performed an in-depth investigation of the electronic properties of SrMnO$_3$ within the DMFT framework. By leveraging a non-self-consistent approach, we were able to utilize the high-quality single-particle spectrum provided by experiments to enhance the efficiency of our calculations. This method overcame the limitations associated with using fictitious frequencies in previous DMFT calculations. Our results revealed that using experimental data led to improved local correlations compared to using simple model Hamiltonians. Additionally, we were able to identify two types of $pd$-hybridizations with distinct locations in the energy scale, as well as a potential DMFT phase transition linked to the stability of atomic-like and delocalized electronic states.

Achieving highly coherent operations between remote atomic ensembles requires precise control of laser frequencies, and this is particularly challenging due to the presence of frequency shifts that can vary across different samples.
