This report outlines the data analysis and production characteristics of various particles and mesons, specifically pions, kaons, protons, $\phi$ mesons, produced in Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.44 TeV.

We've identified the primary obstacle in training high-quality conversation state trackers is label noise in the available training data, an inescapable issue in real-world datasets. While numerous strategies have been proposed for cleaning the data, the vast majority require significant, dataset-specific adjustments. An innovative, noise-aware loss function is presented in this paper, which leverages the hierarchical nature of conversation state labels to automatically learn label reliability without needing significant, dataset-specific adjustments. Our findings demonstrate that this function yields superior results compared to the best existing methods in both laboratory and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the function can be seamlessly integrated with high-quality conversation state tracking models through basic multi-task learning techniques, high-precision state prediction can be achieved with minimal performance degradation in comparison.

In November 2019, large demonstrations in Chile were driven primarily by suboptimal public transportation pricing but quickly evolved to encompass broader social discontent. Given the complex nature of this social unrest, precise modeling is inherently difficult. We developed a simplified simulation, however, by adapting the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered mathematical framework to the circumstances in Chile. This basic model was capable of capturing the essential dynamics of the protests, although more intricate versions might yield an even more accurate portrayal of the demonstrations.

Researchers utilized the VLT in its Compact Very Large Array (VLBA) baseline mode to examine the H- $\alpha$ and H-$\gamma$ emission lines in a sample of 14 galaxies that were fitted with spectral energy distributions (SEDs). By comparing the ratios of these emission lines to H-$\alpha$, a strong correlation with the star-formation rates (SFRs) was found. Notably, galaxies with a temperature of 1000K or less exhibited a stronger link between line ratio and SFR temperature. Through the derivation of the "SFR threshold" for each line, a threshold of $10^{-3} L_{\odot}$ was established for [N III] $\lambda\lambda$5755, 5766. Furthermore, by calculating the "efficiency" $\eta$ for each line, values for [N III] $\lambda\lambda$5755, 5766 and Brackett-$\gamma$ were found to be $1.0 \times 10^{-4}$ and $8.0 \times 10^{-4}$, respectively. Additionally, a method was proposed to derive SFRs from [N III] $\lambda\lambda$5755, 5766 and Br $\gamma$ using $\eta$, which would be most effective for [N III] $\lambda\lambda$5755,

We have a complete and concise proof that localized second-order stochastic processes are on the boundary of the cone of sums of squares. Additionally, we've completed a partial proof that localized hyperbolic polynomials belong to the interior of the SOS cone.

Substantial shifts in neutrino oscillation patterns, not attributable to standard model parameters, are a telltale sign of non-standard neutrino behavior, such as lepton flavor universality violations observed in other experiments. Upcoming high-statistical studies of neutrino oscillations at FASER$
u$ in conjunction with LHC will offer a highly accurate means of detecting any such deviations. Taking into account the characteristics of neutrinos produced in $W$ boson decays to facilitate comprehensive comparisons across experiments, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the impacts of non-standard neutrino interactions on $
u$-induced deep inelastic scattering at FASER$
u$. By estimating possible detection signals for various types of non-standard neutrino interactions through both dimension-6 and dimension-8 operators, we established new constraints that are at least as strict as current limits from COHERENT and other experiments.

Alphabet-based regular expressions with intersection and complement operations can effectively be utilized to represent and manipulate automata languages, thereby simplifying certain automata operations. However, this approach cannot be directly applied to resolve inequalities involving these expressions. To address this limitation, Bruch and Brumley developed a method for solving inequalities by first eliminating the complement operation through the application of automata-based techniques, such as Glushkov's and Aho's transformations. Their原有的方法 suffers from exponential complexity relative to the length of the expressions, which can be overly restrictive in practical applications. This paper introduces an innovative algorithm for resolving such inequalities that avoids the complement operation and achieves O(n) complexity, where n denotes the number of symbols in the expressions. This method also facilitates the extension of expressions with additional operators.

State estimation via visual-inertial odometry (VIO) is a critical component in robotics systems that integrate vision and inertial sensors for seamless navigation. The Profound VO (ProVIO) framework, built on Profound Learning for Real-Time VO (ProFLO11), has set a high benchmark in monocular VIO benchmarks. While the feature extraction module (FEM) of ProVIO relies on the ProFLO11's memory focus module (MFM) to enhance real-time performance, it inherits some limitations from the MFM, including the use of L1 normalization which hinders its visual feature processing. To overcame these constraints, we present the External Memory Attention-based Monocular VIO (EMA-VIO) system, which incorporates an attention-based memory module that allows for seamless integration of any type of external memory. The attention-based memory module effectively allocates the L1 normalization solely to the inertial integration, thereby enabling EMA-VIO to surpass the ProVIO benchmark in accuracy by a significant margin (from 0.137 RPE to 0.083) in the EuRoC dataset without compromising real-time performance. EMA-VIO's design ensures full differentiability, making it highly adaptable to various applications in the fields of robotics and automation.

We propose a novel type of three-dimensional Weyl semimetal called square-root elevated-order Weyl semimetal, and provide two mechanisms in model Hamiltonians that result in this phase. These mechanisms involve derivative relationships between neighboring order-parameter valleys in a valley-crystalline mountain landscape and the anti-commutation of symmetry-required band crossings with an expansion to lower dimensions. The proposed models exhibit both exotic order parameters and conventional descriptors like monopoles in Berry curvature and Chern-Simons conductance when translated to real-space defects. Furthermore, we reveal that the square-root elevated-order Weyl points possess unconventional charge-quantized triads of dipole-monopole and exhibit characteristic square-root singularities in some physical observables. This finding opens the door to exploring the unique properties of square-root textured Berry curvature in three-dimensional condensed matter systems.

This study introduces a novel approach to resolving an inverse boundary value problem in $\mathbb{R}^3$, specifically related to determining the magnetic permeability $\mu$ and electric conductivity $\sigma$ within a bounded domain $\Omega$.  The underlying problem relies on internal measurements of the electric and magnetic fields and boundary measurements of the normal component of the magnetic field.  To solve it, we employ the quasi-reversibility method, which involves reformulating the problem as four first-order boundary value problems.  Our strategy includes a slight modification to an existing method by H. Ammari and C. H. Kwak and also addresses challenges arising from the three-dimensional space.  We present and validate a numerical scheme using a three-dimensional variant of the Q2R2 algorithm.  This includes examples such as a cubic and a spherical domain $\Omega$.

The vertex operator algebra $K(g,k)$ is associated with a Kac-Moody algebra $g$ and is constructed from its universal enveloping algebra. This paper develops a framework to construct certain rational and conformal $N$-parafermion vertex operator algebras, specifically focusing on Lie superalgebras. By parameterizing the universality of $N$-parafermion vertex operator algebras over simple Lie superalgebras at affine level $k$, the paper establishes an instance for $g=$ $osp(1|2n)$ and derives the conformal weights of its irreducible modules. Additionally, it identifies the $F_k(osp(1|2n))$ as the block category of Witten's twisted $\beta\gamma$-shear category with representation spaces as irreducible highest weight modules of affine $osp(1|2n)$ with integer affine levels.

The vast amount of data stored in cloud systems has kept it isolated, preventing effective sharing and collaboration. In contrast, several organizations now have access to data in multiple formats, enabling seamless integration. To bridge this gap, Federated Learning offers a possible solution, yet it faces significant computational challenges when dealing with large datasets. Our research proposes a novel approach called FLRA that allows multiple organizations to collaborate without directly sharing their data, thereby avoiding data privacy breaches. FLRA employs a discriminative learning technique to create a robust and high-quality knowledge graph, ensuring its credibility through a feedback loop.

In the mammalian entorhinal cortex, grid cells were first identified and are known to generate a coordinate system that encompasses various spatial information, potentially guiding the hippocampus. This review explores the properties of grid cells and the research surrounding them, with an emphasis on neurophysiological studies in awake animals. We discuss how place cells are affected by vestibular stimulation, the role of entorhinal inputs to the hippocampus in memory, and possible hippocampal-hippocampal and hippocampus-entorhinal communication mechanisms. Additionally, we examine theoretical models of grid cell behavior. The research reviewed highlights robust features of grid cells, such as stable grid patterns, orientation, scale, and phase across sessions and during boundary movements. We observe that most hippocampal decoding models assume a grid-coordinate feedback mechanism. The majority of current grid cell formation models are place-cell-based, with models utilizing linear threshold neurons and plasticity rules influenced by entorhinal and hippocampal interactions. The majority of these models produce grid cells through a two-stage process, comprising the formation of a "bimodal" intermediate state. Furthermore, we highlight recent advances in the development of grid cells through a grid-cell-direct model. The model described results in grid cells upon applying a grid-pattern-oriented state to an auto-associative network.

This paper explores how differential rotation affects a star's spin as it matures and considers its role in generating magnetic fields during this process. We developed an adaptation of a previously used model to understand this phenomenon in rotating stars. Using this model, we calculated the electric fields induced by differential rotation in a star that is present at the main sequence and is rotating on its axis. We used a magnetic vector that is symmetric around the star's axis to represent this induction and found that it decreases as the star matures and its differential rotation-induced field could be responsible for observed magnetic cycles in G-type stars. These calculations were further analyzed using magnetohydrodynamic simulations of Nernst waves in a star that is present at the main sequence and is rotating on its axis, which confirmed that the axial magnetic field decreases as the star matures and is consistent with our magnetic vector's predictions. This implies that differential rotation in a rotating star can generate long-lasting magnetic cycles and could contribute to magnetic environments on these planets as they are present.

Using computational methods, we examine the statistical distribution of elliptic curve rank within certain quartic fields ($S_4$ and $A_4$) and their respective Galois invariant subsets. Our analysis involves calculating the rank of approximately 65,000 elliptic curves across all possible quartic fields up to a specific discriminant limit. These calculations are then used to estimate the frequency of rank development patterns among subsets of elliptic curves in $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions of the rational numbers.

Our research reveals how quantum thermal states behave in the context of quantum field theories that align with certain holographic principles. By applying geometry-based techniques and numerical simulations, we investigated how quantum thermal states respond to sudden changes, or quantum quenches, and identified key factors that determine whether entanglement can spread within those states. Our findings show that a specific ratio of temperature to acceleration sets a limit on the acceleration at which this entanglement spread occurs. Additionally, we discovered that the thermal behavior of quantum quenches can be understood through the interaction between two different types of wave propagation. This quantum thermal phase transition is characterized by a specific, dimensionless ratio of acceleration and temperature that we calculated using both analytical methods and numerical simulations.

Quantum velocity limits and discriminability have shared the same mathematical foundation since their discovery of the links between them in various systems since their discovery. This study seeks to identify a general criteria for both in any state evolution process, specifically in binary processes within the Bloch sphere. We have developed a new monotone, the asymmetry monotone, capable of capturing both criteria. As demonstration, we applied it to derive both in multiple scenarios, including the optimal velocity for distinguishing two unambiguous states under multiple constraints such as fidelity, smoothness, and chord length, as well as achieving the optimal velocity for discriminability in qutrit systems.

The paper discusses a specific interpolation operator related to a given subset of the unit circle, and provides an upper bound for the ratio of the norm of a function after passing through the subset, to the original norm of the function. The upper bound is set at 2 times the square root of the cardinality of the subset, and it is proven that the bound cannot be improved beyond the order of n^(1/2). Additionally, the paper indicates that certain results derived from Riesz products lead to a concentration phenomenon, where the majority of functions with a specific cardinality subset, exhibit the behavior of their L-infinity norm after passing through the subset, to be approximately proportional to the original norm of the function, multiplied by the square root of the cardinality of the subset.

We utilize terahertz nano-scopic imaging to investigate the electric field distributions within superconducting niobium resonators at various resonant frequencies. By applying this imaging technique, we can experimentally verify the theoretical predictions for capacitor intensity in a frequency-dependent manner. Furthermore, our measurements allow us to visually observe the modes of both a semi-harmonic oscillator and a photonic crystal cavity.

Recently, various versions of curved $K$-theory have gained significant interest in algebraic geometry. This field of study explores the properties of algebraic varieties across different fields. Our research contributes to this area by introducing a motivic counterpart to curved $K$-theory. Specifically, we define an invariant in the homotopy category of a 1-truncated motivic spectrum and prove that it aligns with existing definitions of curved $K$-theory in certain contexts. Additionally, our work facilitates the examination of interesting questions regarding algebraic varieties, such as those related to curvature and the behavior of $K$-theory in different dimensions.

A mathematical model is suggested to model the extended-term development of a planetary atmosphere, taking into account additional processes and feedback mechanisms. The model incorporates changes in solar radiation over time, rock cycle feedback on carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, and temperature effects on meteorite dissolution, as well as differences in meteorite efficacy at various temperatures. The model is then applied to the evolution of Venus\' atmosphere under sudden exposure to the sun after being shielded by their parent planet, and also examines potential implications for Mars\' future atmospheric conditions.

Using ultrafast x-rays, this study tracks the nanoscale movements of molecules in a glycol droplet as they are broken apart by an UV laser, a process that is faster than a molecular vibration. By combining x-ray imaging and spectroscopy, researchers observe nanoseconds of reaction dynamics and how the glycol molecule's electron cloud is reorganized, which in turn affects the glycol's ion emission. The findings provide a visual insight into electron-hole interactions and can be used as a foundation for developing glycol-based photovoltaics.

Recent research has established a connection between matrix product states and a class of quantum circuits, which led to the development of various forms of quantum MPS representations. In this work, we introduce the concept of decomposing an MPS into a product of three distinct types of superficial quantum circuits. Demonstrating the uniqueness of this decomposition under specific constraints, we further show that any given MPS can be expressed through this decomposition via three separate mappings. Ultimately, these results provide a meaningful basis for utilizing the super-circuit approach in investigating complex systems comprising multiple interacting parts.

The rise of whole slide imaging (WSI) as a modality in digital pathology is transforming how pathological examination and research are conducted, despite historical limitations in WSI's spatial and color depth when compared to optical microscopy. Recent advancements in WSI analysis methods overcame these barriers by first extracting thousands of image patches for pathological evaluation, yet this approach no longer applies to deep learning models required for task-specific WSIs tasks. To address these challenges, researchers have explored hierarchical neural network architectures that integrate multi-scale features and contextual WSIs information, showcasing improved performance in various tasks. In this survey, the authors provide an in-depth exploration of hierarchical neural network representations in WSIs analysis, including their components, functionalities, implementations, and applications such as cancer diagnosis and prognosis, as well as other medical imaging tasks. The researchers also discuss the challenges in this domain and their perspectives on potential future advancements.

We present a novel, non-linear maxwellian Hawkes model and a corresponding non-parametric Bayesian evaluation method. Our approach utilizes an independent prior for the influence matrix and meticulously analyzes the posterior distribution to derive confidence intervals for key parameters, including the baseline rate, exponential waiting time parameters, and the influence matrix. We demonstrate our method's applicability by examining the Twitter discussions surrounding the 2019 World Championships in Swimming. Our developed models are open-source and available for public use on GitHub.

This paper builds on previous work introduced in [1], specifically addressing the inconsistency in angular momentum preservation observed in RMRT [1]. We identify and rectify an error in the calculation of the multipole potential within the described framework, ensuring accurate angular momentum preservation. Furthermore, we extend the algorithm's capabilities to accommodate negative integer values of l.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks-based segmentation methods have generally achieved high accuracy, they struggle with domain adaptation, particularly when adapting to images captured under low-quality conditions, such as single-phase CT. This challenge stems from the fact that low-quality images display altered texture and intensity patterns compared to high-quality images. We hypothesize that by introducing an element of competition during the training process, the model can preserve anatomical consistency despite these significant differences. We propose a novel two-stage domain adaptation framework, consisting of initial cross-domain knowledge transfer and subsequent region-specific learning. During the knowledge transfer stage, target images are divided into multiple regions and each is matched with a corresponding source image region containing the same organ. These source regions are then fine-tuned using the transferred knowledge to minimize the discrepancy between the target and source regions. However, this is an overly simplified approach and does not fully account for the complex domain adaptation process.

The success of the effective field theory method can be partially attributed to the 1.5 order framework, which generally ensures that the gauge symmetries in a theory remain consistent as it moves from the classical to the quantum realm. Unfortunately, the 1.5 order framework appears to create an inconsistency with a theory of minimally coupled supergravity, as applying the framework yields a non-nilpotent BRS transformation when examined more closely. Investigating this issue reveals that the 1.5 order framework might be flawed, as it disregards a crucial term in the path integral formulation, which represents an infinitesimal gauge transformation of the gravitino field. rectifying this omission generates a fully consistent, albeit more complex, nilpotent BRS transformation for minimally coupled supergravity.

A 20-petawatt laser system, consisting of two synchronized pulses with opposite circular polarizations, is enhanced as it passes through a plasma medium, where one polarization is selectively absorbed, resulting in up to an 11-petawatt circularly polarized peak. This process maintains an extremely high quality factor for interacting with plasma, allowing for an improved outcome compared to vacuum conditions, where the polarizations would rapidly cancel each other out over the same interaction length. Furthermore, it's evident from theory and simulations that varying the magnetization of the plasma enables precise control over the output's absorption and field ionization processes, particularly in two-photon ionization, opening up the possibility of controlling the electron emission pattern and field.

Using updated world data from shape analyses of differential differential cross-sections, we have obtained precise values for the electroweak form factors $|F_W(\tau^+ \tau^-)|$. At $q^2 = 0$, the Re $F_\Phi(0)$ values are found to be $0.0104 \pm 0.0004$ for $0.5~\text{GeV}^2 \leq q^2 \leq 4.6~\\text{GeV}^2$, $0.0104 \pm 0.0004$ for $4.6~\text{GeV}^2 \leq q^2 \leq 55.7~\text{GeV}^2$, and $0.0154 \pm 0.0005$ for $60.0~\text{GeV}^2 \leq q^2 \leq 91.2~\text{GeV}^2$, with an overall combined uncertainty of $8\%$. The imaginary part of $F_\Phi(0)$ has a value of $0.0084 \pm 0.0004$, resulting in a total magnitude of $|F_\Phi(0)| = 0.0154 \pm 0.0005$. These

Error correction in optical data storage, specifically in CRW and PW-DVD formats, relies on identifying and correcting rank errors in 2D binary matrices representing stored information. This paper introduces an algorithm capable of correcting an entire class of errors known as symmetric rank errors by combining existing methods and leveraging the structural properties of the matrices representing video and audio data. Our proposed approach yields a more robust solution, outperforming the current error correction standards in both CRW and PW-DVD formats.

In the context of three-dimensional conformal field theory, especially within the e-fold boundary, additional symmetries permit the streamlining of four-point operator product expansions by aligning certain primary operators along a common trajectory. In this configuration, the contribution of any given primary to the correlation function's spectrum becomes governed by just two parameters rather than four. Our objective is to explore the feasibility of implementing this simplification for the SO(2,2) symmetries, also known as SL(2,R)xSL(2,R), symmetry group. Moreover, we will present the necessary conditions under which such a setup can be satisfied for these symmetries in both massless and gapped CFTs while preserving unitarity. Our primary findings are the derivation of differential equations that any massless scalar's contribution to the stress-energy T(z)s correlation function must satisfy, as well as the demonstration that, in the massless scenario, existing solutions to these equations either exhibit non-unitary behavior or correspond to well-documented families of functions. In the gapped scenario, we further simplify the corresponding differential equations under the condition that the CFT in question exhibits a gap, allowing us to characterize an extensive class of theories that exhibit this property.

Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure the intensity of gravity's impact on the CMB with high precision. To achieve this, it's crucial to understand how this effect is imposed. One approach involves using machine learning to create an inverse model, which could potentially extract information about the effect that was removed from the observed data. In this study, we examine whether such an inverse model is capable of recovering the effect on the CMB when there are tensor modes present, which would otherwise contaminate the model. Our results indicate that while our experiment is feasible under certain conditions, the residual effects on the CMB when present would still be within the range of what experiments can measure, typically at a level of a few times the expected noise level. To further clarify this, we propose a specific strategy for analyzing data that takes into account any unaccounted effects on the CMB.

In 1972, Gelfand and MacPherson developed a recursive method for calculating Pontrjagin classes. Their approach involved selecting a compact subset within a real vector space and determining the associated filtration of Grassmannian varieties. We are grateful to Chris Elliott for sharing his insights which helped us revise and refine our research.

We analyzed multi-epoch photometric data and nearly 20 H$\beta$ and [O I] spectral snapshots of SN 2020jfo, a Type II-S supernova, from days 6 to 330 after explosion. Based on the light curve and spectroscopic characteristics, SN 2020jfo displayed a normal range of properties. Its global light curve, as well as its color evolution, mirrored that of other normal SN II with short plateaus. Additionally, the [O I] spectrum and its strength matched typical behavior of this class. However, SN 2020jfo occurred in a sub-solar metallicity environment and had an orbiting companion with the potential to influence its dynamics.

To broaden the field of view for elliptical focal surface lenses in X-ray telescopes, we propose adding a second lens array with intermixed orientation, effectively creating a multi-focal surface design. This concept is illustrated using scientific lobster-eye lens technology. By calculating the light-capturing area and spatial resolution for a two-fold lens array, we find that approximately 40% of incoming X-rays are focused onto the focal surface, resulting in the reconstruction of the source's field of view with a spatial resolution of 10's of arcminutes. Although the project's parameters are not optimized, this approach could still allow for the detection of high-energy transients like gamma-ray bursts and gravitational waves across a wide field of view, or even lead to the creation of broad-field X-ray telescopes.

We establish a stage-set version of partial uniform ellipticity and the associated Harnack inequality that rely solely on boundary values of coefficients. This involves estimating the 'distance' between quadratic forms through their action on stage sets, and yields the desired results through monotonicity arguments. Our approach may be seen as an alternative to intrinsic scaling methods, though it is noted that some uniform isomorphism assumptions on stage sets appear challenging to apply to time-dependent scenarios.

The concept of the cosmic speed field (CSF), first proposed a century ago by de Sadeleer, has never been rigorously analyzed due to a lack of direct evidence. In a surprising finding involving a relatively rare type of galaxy known as isolated spirals, our research reveals that the CSF appears to exist as a distinct, continuous layer within their halos. Through numerical simulations and real observational data, we've discovered that the characteristics of this CSF region vary significantly, leading to the formation of different dark matter halo profiles and, as a result, a range of galaxy distributions in the mass realm. Notably, identifying the boundaries of the CSF field has been discovered to provide the most efficient path to achieving a precise description of the dark matter halo structure in isolated spiral galaxies, rather than relying on traditional methods such as the rotation curve alone.

This paper proposes a novel method for automatic musical keyboard transcription using semi-supervised convolutive non-negative matrix factorization. This method utilizes a small set of annotated recordings to train a model that can accurately transpose any piece of music onto a virtual keyboard. The proposed system first generates a large dataset of artificial recordings based on a small set of real ones, and then trains a model using convolutive NMF. Experimental results show that this method obtains state-of-the-art performance on the challenging MD100 evaluation task, achieving a mean score of 4.66, and also yields excellent results on an automatic musical score generation task, outperforming several baseline methods.

We have developed a new method for developing rotating stars in both special and general relativity by using cylindrical coordinates and developing configurations gradually via Lagrangian mass coordinates. This methodology enables us to create realistic models of rotating stars, taking into account the forces of cohesion present within them. As an example, we used this method to develop a series of realistic models of rotating stars in flat spacetime, based on Barotropic equations of state commonly found in literature, demonstrating that our results are consistent with existing results from especially the Maeder book, yet in a simpler and more straightforward manner. Furthermore, our findings also imply that any rotating star in flat spacetime will eventually collapse into a barotropic equation of state, similar to the one described by Bardeen and Glacken (1947).

A cutting-edge document intelligence framework is proposed to automatically identify and interpret complex documents, which is particularly useful in scenarios involving financially intricate reports. Realizing this proposal demands a state-of-the-art deep learning model trained on a large dataset. One significant hurdle in achieving this is acquiring high-quality data labels for visually rich documents. Manual labeling, although accurate, becomes impractical and expensive when applied to massive datasets. To overcome this challenge, this paper presents a novel approach to obtaining high-quality labeled datasets. It employs state-of-the-art detection and recognition models to label large datasets, with subsequent human review focused on correcting inaccurate labels rather than initial labeling. This method significantly reduces the human labor required, with human participants tasked with validating model-generated labels. The proposed approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments, with results showing substantial time and cost savings in labeling tasks. The resulting high-quality dataset successfully trains a reliable and high-performance document intelligence framework. The system's performance is comparable to that achieved using manually labeled datasets. Furthermore, this framework is designed to be modular, with the ability to integrate with existing detection and recognition models. It is also adaptable to a wide range of documents, from business financial reports to personal tax forms. The proposed approach is implemented within the M-DLEF system, with the source code publicly accessible on GitHub.

The mergers of neutron stars and black holes produce gravitational waves that carry a wealth of information, including the potential signatures of a neutron star's demise as it approaches a black hole's event horizon.  By studying these gravitational waves, scientists gain insight into the fundamental properties of both the neutron star and the black hole.  However, analyzing neutron star-signature gravitational waves poses significant challenges due to their rarity and the vast parameters of possible outcomes.  In this study, we present initial findings on using deep learning techniques to identify and classify these distinctive gravitational wave patterns through a newly generated data library encompassing a wide range of neutron star models merging with black holes of various masses.  We successfully designed neural networks that can accurately distinguish neutron star signatures from black hole-only mergers and different types of gravitational wave signals, achieving high precision at specific signal-to-noise ratios.  Our results reveal that lower-dimensional classifier networks may not be ideal for this task due to their limited capacity to capture the complex nature of these gravitational wave patterns.  Instead, we found that a code-based approach yields superior performance, enabling a precise classification of the merging neutron star and black hole masses.  Our discoveries also indicate that certain neutron star models may not be distinguishable from black hole-only mergers due to the absence of characteristic tidal effects in the gravitational wave signal.

The availability of reliable public health data is often hindered by sensitive information that can be inferred from text, which is a major challenge in social learning. Social learning can be achieved by predicting and influencing the attitudes of others, a process that can be applied to settings such as social media. In this paper, we propose a novel token-based neural network that uses the BERT language model to extract sensitive information from text. Our framework is flexible and can be tailored to target specific social issues by incorporating different types of training data. We evaluated our model on the task of identifying public health-related text on Facebook, achieving higher accuracy compared to existing methods. Notably, we discovered that the tone of the text can be effectively learned from example labels. Furthermore, we discovered that non-sensitive keywords can be effective features for training classifiers. Based on these findings, we propose a new entity extraction task called Token Entity Extraction (TEE) and introduce the (Facebook) Medicine Dataset (FMD), a high-quality dataset of medical entities extracted from text on Facebook social media. Our results demonstrate that our proposed token-based neural network is effective at identifying the intended social issue in text, outperforming existing baselines.

This paper delves into the optimal movement of a scallop in a viscous fluid, as modeled by a resistive force law. The model is applied to understand how a biolumphic animal like a scallop can filter for food. A key feature of this model is its ability to account for the different drag forces experienced by the scallop's valves due to their varying sizes and surface areas. The optimal movement of the scallop is a complex balance between filtering for food, self-propulsion, and minimizing the energy expended. A key insight is that, for a given opening speed, there exists an optimal closure speed that maximizes food intake. The research presented in this paper is a set of intricate, high-dimensional scenarios that are useful for understanding the optimal movement of a scallop and related bio-fluid dynamic systems. The research presented in this paper is a set of intricate, high-dimensional scenarios that are useful for numerical algorithms to find a solution.

A global pandemic significantly disrupts social engagements and has profound, uneven socio-economic repercussions in cities worldwide. Researchers utilize mobile device data to study how individuals' movements change during pandemics, revealing substantial variations across urban areas and persistent shifts post-pandemic. Furthermore, analysis of mobile phone data shows that pandemic-induced shifts in movements correlate strongly with pre-existing economic disparities, leading to differential impacts on various sectors of society. Utilizing this insight, we develop an adjusted version of entropy, a commonly used metric for quantifying social mobility in cities, that accounts for both mobility disparities and directional changes in movements. We demonstrate that this refined entropy function can effectively model the behavioral patterns observed during the COVID-19 pandemic across numerous global urban centers, outperforming simpler models such as the original entropy function and Gaussian distributions.

Observations suggest that massive young stars exist within dense regions and are often found in association with gas outflows and mergers.  A new numerical simulation involving three dimensions and general relativity has been conducted to understand how these massive young stars form and develop.  This simulation merged existing techniques for resolving gravitational collapse in simulation with a technique called adaptive mesh refinement used to extend the simulation's timeline.  Results indicate that two separate flows of gas are present in the simulation: one that spirals inward due to angular momentum and another that moves radially outward due to angular momentum.  This results in an intermittent accretion pattern, characterized by alternating spiral and radial gas flows, leading to the formation of an elliptical accretion disk and spiral arms.  A new numerical experiment has been conducted to understand the impact of angular momentum on accretion patterns, leading to similar results in which massive young stars form and merge in isolation.  However, in the experiment with tidal forces included, gas outflows become more obvious and visible, leading to the formation of an elliptical star after two separate mergers.  This indicates that an elliptical shape is common in simulations of gas dynamics and that it may be observed in gas outflows.  This simulation also leads to a reevaluation of previous assumptions about how massive young stars form and develop, leading to the conclusion that episodic accretion, gas outflows, and mergers are all essential components of the process.

Building upon the method of wedge-local Hamiltonians, a framework is established to analyze open systems within the 2d Minkowski space using endomorphisms defined by Longo-Witten. A key result derived from this framework is the expression of a wedge-local Hamiltonian in terms of the Longo-Witten endomorphisms across a range of interactions, including massless and massive scenarios, both rational and irreducible. A path towards determining the Longo-Witten endomorphisms from the wedge-local Hamiltonian is also investigated. Furthermore, the connection between the algebraic spin and the underlying modular data of a rational conformal field theory is extended to the endomorphisms. The expression of the mass gap in terms of the underlying modular data is further explored.

The rapid expansion of 5G technology has been fueled by government promotion and the growing necessity of high-speed, low-latency 5G networks. Despite numerous studies exploring various socioeconomic aspects of digital adoption, research on children's exposure to 5G masts as a digital dividend has not received much attention. This paper fills that knowledge gap and aims to examine how often children and vital medical establishments are exposed to 5G masts in neighboring areas. It also investigates exposure levels during critical times of the day in regions with multiple 5G masts, primarily focusing on two highly populated counties in England. To achieve this, it utilizes open-source software to analyze mobile signal data and employs a reliable model for accurate exposure estimation. The results from these analysis methods are then discussed. Ultimately, the study seeks to balance the advantages of digital inclusion with the well-being of children and medical institutions, emphasizing the importance of managing 5G exposure as a positive byproduct of digital development.

We have developed a Hamiltonian Dysthe approximation for three-dimensional deep-water gravity waves that start from a region of constant vorticity. Our approach involves adapting Dysthe's semi-circle transformation to create new variables that linearize the water's surface equations under specific conditions. By applying this linearity, we have derived both exact and asymptotic expressions for the average vorticity within a specific range of non-dimensional parameters. Our study also presents new figures illustrating how vorticity behaves as these parameters change, and as they converge to zero, linking our results to the Dysthe bell curve. Additionally, our research extends Dysthe's work on vortex cores and provides a Hamiltonian framework for his numerical simulations.

We introduce a novel framework for locally arching spaces, a theoretical model that allows us to generalize and extend the concepts of arching spaces. This new framework is then utilized to define a class of differential structures on locally arching spaces. These defined structures encompass arching spaces as a subset. We have also developed a modified version of the arching space arching lemma applicable to locally arching spaces. This modification, along with our definitions of morphisms and differential forms, enables us to prove a Stokes theorem on locally arching spaces. This proof is possible because the arching space arching lemma has been extended to these spaces.

This research focuses on developing a control system for a drone that uses sonar data to navigate through multiple layers in a structured environment. By utilizing sonar sensors, the drone can efficiently navigate within a stratified space as a result of its navigation controller. A simple model was created to test the performance of the control system on a quadrotor, simulating three distinct layers of obstacles. A performance assessment was conducted by analyzing the path traced, navigation time, and energy used. The results revealed that the control system achieved successful path following within the environment, resulting in a 31.7% improvement in navigation speed compared to a previous baseline, while avoiding collisions, as evidenced by a sonar reading above a 0.25m safety margin.

News literacy has faced significant challenges in the true/false classification
of modernchallenging and deceptive news articles due to their intricate nature. To
address this issue, we investigated the efficacy of text summarization models in
assisting with true/false classification of news articles. To begin with, we
compiled a comprehensive dataset encompassing 100k China Jouals news articles
from July 2020 to July 2021. Subsequently, we employed three summarization models
to condense 30k randomly selected articles from each class, and then applied these
summarization models to the remaining 70k articles for true/false classification.
Experimental results revealed the capability of utilizing text summarization models
for true/false classification of news articles, with different summarization models
yielding varied outcomes. Furthermore, we analyzed the influence of auxiliary
information, dataset scale, and distribution on summarization models' performance.
Moreover, we discovered that leveraging a super-visioned guide from multi-model
ensembling of original, BERT-based, and contrastive learning models improved
summarization models' performance. Additionally, we found that leveraging
metadata and multi-task learning could enhance the true/false classification
performance of summarization models.

The stochastic dynamics occurring on complex surfaces hold significance in various scientific fields and are frequently modeled using heat equations. The development of such models depends crucially on the curvature of the underlying surface. In this study, the impact of Riemannian curvature is explored through a series of examples involving Gaussian stochastic fields. The curvature's influence is shown to have measurable effects, including a distinct acceleration or deceleration in the mean-square displacement and a modifying effect on the displacement distribution over time. Notably, similar outcomes are achieved through a technique involving the decomposition of a Gaussian field into independent components, each evolving at different rates. The approach is further refined by introducing an inverse square law surface, in which this disintegration effect alone can account for the observed changes in mean-square displacement. The findings presented in this study are illustrated using simulated data and may have implications for interpreting surface-based analyses of multivariate time series that exhibit complex dynamics.

The implementation of Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) increases signal efficiency and system capacity but also amplifies the noise in the system, posing a threat of malicious users interfering with legitimate users in wireless communications. Researchers have developed an overlay-coded NOMA (Co-NOMA) approach, allowing nominal users to use an outer code to encrypt their signals, reducing the decoding errors due to malicious users. In this letter, a decentralized method is introduced to decode the nominal users' overlay codes in a self-resolving manner, eliminating the need for pilot signals or decoding assistance from base stations. The proposed technique demonstrates successful code decoding for nominal users in multiple scenarios, exhibiting up to 1.5-dB performance gain over the conventional separated decoding method.

When working with large-scale datasets, it is essential to be able to evaluate the first principal component (PC1) of a rotationally symmetric $\ell_1$-norm cloud efficiently. This paper introduces a projection method for calculating the PC1 of such a symmetric cluster. Specifically, it demonstrates that, under certain conditions, the algorithm can produce a solution within a fixed number of steps, indicating linear convergence. A key feature of this approach is its ability to leverage precomputed quantities from the dataset to optimize performance. Nonetheless, the convergence criteria established in this research are more stringent than those established for standard $2$-norm PC problems. This limitation raises the question of whether a comparable approach can be applied to rotationally symmetric clusters in the $2$-norm norm.

In the context of online communities, users frequently seek emotional support through their posts, which social assistants can facilitate by identifying and labeling emotions. Existing emotion-labeling methods fall short in accuracy and coverage, necessitating a more reliable approach. This research proposes a unique framework that utilizes pre-trained BERT to generate high-quality emotion labels for data with limited or inaccurate annotations. By leveraging a combination of deep learning classification models and rule-based methods, this framework can process and validate a diverse range of annotations, resulting in a significant improvement in the reliability and efficiency of emotion-labeling for online text data.
The traditional theory of power verbs and attributes applies to ordered groups, especially those within the domain of abelian groups with a natural ordering.

As 11-minute X-ray pulsors represent a distinct class of X-ray binary systems, their primary feature is an X-ray emission that syncs with the accreting object's rotation period. As asynchronous polars, these systems X-ray emissions don't connect with the binary systems X-ray binary systems X-ray emissions can vary dramatically during their 1-11 minute light curves. Some systems exhibit bi-modal or even tri-modal distributions of X-ray emissions. Furthermore, the systems' X-ray emissions softest state is often observed. Conversely, non-synchronous polars exhibit softer X-ray emissions. This comparison between asynchronous and non-synchronous polars reveals no notable distinction in their average X-ray spectra hardness.

This work introduces two innovative reduction methods for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems. We consider the standard FSI framework, which involves the structural boundary moving in response to the surrounding fluid. The first approach, a fully coupled method, utilizes a segmentable Reduced Basis formulation based on the Oldroyd-Alpha method. This approach enables the simultaneous solution of the fluid and structural problems through a fully coupled solver, which we develop by combining the Oliger's subgrid technique with a block diagonal Jacobian linearization. The method is complemented by a reliable a posteriori estimation of the reduction method's global error. The approach yields precise results for linear problems and provides satisfactory outcomes for nonlinear cases. The second approach divides the problem into separate stages: a Lagrangian Reduced Basis method for the structural component and a moving grid Reduced Basis method for the fluid, which we develop using a projection-based version of the Arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian technique. The method's efficiency is demonstrated through the simulation of a classic FSI problem.

Building navigation in the real world using camera input and LiDAR data is a complex task for robots. A key aspect of this challenge lies in representing the environment. A map that captures the topological features of an environment is essential for a robot to plan and execute efficient navigation. Current representations, while useful, have limitations when it comes to providing a comprehensive and concise overview of the environment, which can hinder effective navigation. To address this, we propose a novel approach called HiTMap, a hierarchical topological diagram representation for 2D environments. HiTMap combines detailed, globally aligned cylindrical segments with a grid representation, which facilitates efficient local path planning. A subset of our proposed HiTMap structure can be used for navigation in unfamiliar environments, as demonstrated by our results using simulation and real-world data.

Offensive language in social media can spread rapidly due to its echo chamber effect. Our goal is to detect tweets with racist or homophobic content for the SemEval-2019 Task on Offensiveness and Stereotyping. We are participating in this task from the University of Massachusetts Amherst and Iowa State University, having entered the competition with 4 teams in total. During the challenge, we also tackled a related task, specifically a binary classification of racist content. Our main framework involved combining two types of detectors, a traditional machine learning model and a modern BERT-based one, with the traditional model correctly identifying the majority of tweets, while the BERT model identified more, but with lower accuracy, leading to the final model's accuracy depending on how we weighted the traditional model's predictions. By adjusting the traditional model's threshold, we were able to significantly improve our F1 score, especially in the evaluation with 10 classes, where our score was 4 points higher than the baseline. All our code and results are openly available on GitHub.

Employing a compact atomic interferometry system linked to radio frequency technology, we've developed a highly sensitive method for measuring minute changes in local magnetic fields. By leveraging the Meissner effect in a superconducting coil, we can expel and trap atomic radio frequency fields, offering a sensitive detection method. Our system's detection range covers both low and high frequency regions, and can be tailored to optimize the detection of specific frequencies. Notably, our setup achieves a level of sensitivity equivalent to $27~\mathrm{nT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ across a wide $2~\mathrm{kHz}$ band when utilizing the Meissner effect, equivalent to $9~\mathrm{nT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ at $2~\mathrm{kHz}$ when radio frequency fields are increased to the edge of detectability. By directly manipulating the trapping conditions of the radio frequency fields, we can adjust the effective area of interaction and control the detection sensitivity, thus providing a customizable approach for different applications and requirements.

The distinctive properties of two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals crystals can be modified by altering their atomic arrangement into moiré patterns, a process known as superlattices formation. Leveraging this, our study reveals the possibility of achieving close-range magnetic order and spin-polarized magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). Specifically, we demonstrate that a closure of the antiferromagnetic order in an MoTe$_2$ monolayer due to strain leads to a strain-induced close-range ferromagnetic order, spin-polarized MCE, and a closure of the bandgap at the Fermi level. As a result, this system exhibits ferromagnetic metal characteristics with spin-polarized magnetocaloric effect (MCE) as a function of strain, providing a pathway for strain-controlled magnetic metals with MCE in 2D TMDs, which may have significant technological applications in magnetic refrigeration technology and thermoelectric devices utilizing magnetic materials.

A novel scheme is proposed for confining light within a gap between a metal and dielectric, realising gap-plasmons. We examine these states, particularly in terms of outflowing electrons from the metal surface, and the impact of nonlocality on their behavior. We investigate how these factors modify the states' localization length and resonance frequency. A significant modification is found for states with small energy, or those occurring near the Fermi energy. In contrast, a theoretical state was analyzed where the metal's dielectric function incorporates both nonlocality and outflowing electrons. We discovered that a certain metal model, characterized by finite speed of light and spatial dispersion of its electrons, can exhibit gap-plasmons similar to those predicted by local theories.

The addition of normal forms to the Calculus of Constructions with Inductive
Types significantly speeds up normalization but causes loss of type information.
We develop a robust normalization process for CCI that utilizes an extended
kernel syntax to preserve normal forms while maintaining 5-level confluence.
These normal forms can be manipulated as terms without prematurely evaluating
encapsulated computations, a feature essential for coinductive proof construction.
Our approach has been given coinductive big-step semantics and supported by three
model checks.

The rise of machine learning techniques for analyzing complex systems has underscored the necessity of a meaningful interpretation of extracted concepts. To achieve this, a methodical framework called Topological Quantum Occurrence Decomposition (TQOD) was developed, leveraging simple theoretical models such as the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. In doing so, TQOD successfully identified and verified key topological features, including the polarization pattern, while also revealing the significance of energy level spacing. Furthermore, the successful application of the TQOD method to this model lays the groundwork for its adaptation to more intricate systems, even those beyond classical computation, such as quantum many-body systems and photonic structures.

A high-performance mobile robot navigation system is designed to detect and avoid obstacles in dynamic environments using a laser range finder, and a method for assessing the performance of this system involves creating a simulated environment with a ground truth model. To do this, we combine elements of stochastic geometry and theory with the result that performance metrics can be expressed as a function of shape parameters, as shown by Klain and Meyer. However, representing complex objects as finite unions of non-overlapping spheres or convex shapes significantly restricts the applicability of this theory. Overcoming this limitation, a statistical model based on finite mixtures allows the modelled object to be described as the envelope of multiple random spheres. The model's parameters can be estimated using a well-established method, the Expectation Maximization algorithm.

We derive the four-point amplitude for gravitons in AdS$_5$ within two-loop order using dimensional regularization, maintaining the non-gauge-invariant structure of the tree-level diagram. This approach bypasses the complications of integrating out intermediate modes across different momentum shells, which typically plague perturbative QFT in AdS spaces. By directly applying the obtained amplitude to the computation of anomalous dimensions for half-BPS operators, we confirm previous findings while using a distinct methodology. Furthermore, we identify and categorize finite QFT contributions arising at even-loop orders in certain operator mixing sectors, namely those originating from 't Hooft coupling and theta-angle renormalizations, and we predict the structure of infinite-loop anomalous dimension matrix entries based on their perturbative forms.

High-performance computing on SRAT-based GPUs demands efficient use of limited global memory, especially for memory-intensive applications like scientific simulations and multimedia processing. However, existing memory allocators either lack object support, require data structure reorganization, or generate excessive kernels that compromise performance by creating excessive memory tiles. In this study, we introduce a novel, object-based concurrent memory allocator called DynaSOAr on top of MSRA, which allows direct storage of Python objects in global memory. By introducing a new tile-based reference count mechanism and an optimized mark-sweep garbage collector, we address the limitations of traditional GC methods. Our allocator significantly reduces runtime overhead and enhances execution efficiency, as demonstrated in our benchmarks where our techniques outperform existing alternatives in various GPU programming languages and libraries, including Minecraft and COMSOL.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse class of sublinear operators along with their commutators on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, sufficient conditions for the boundedness of these operators and commutators on these spaces are established.

Using a first-principles approach based on initial principles of relativistic many-body theory and the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov model, we explore two systems: a single Mn adatom and a dimer of Mn atoms on the Nb(110) surface. Calculations of local density of states and scattering phase curves for both systems show that the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states have a dual origin. These states arise from both the spin-exchange interaction and single-particle levels that are pulled down by the superconductor. For the single Mn adatom, stronger magnetic fields expose more details of the underlying metallic surface. In contrast, magnetic moments of Mn in the Mn dimer are largely canceled due to antiferromagnetic interactions. As a result, the magnetic field has a reduced impact on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states of the Mn dimer.

Our proposed FourierMask achieves instance segmentation as a implicit function, utilizing FourierMapping to map spatial coordinates to regression values for color. By incorporating a FourierMask as a condition along with depth and camera matrix, FourierMask predicts color values for objects. We test the model with synthetic data, achieving a high intersection over union but anticipate similar performance in real-world scenarios.

Let $M$ be a compact, oriented surface with the boundary consisting of $k$ disjoint components in the plane. If $M$ has a smooth, orientation-preserving Hamiltonian immersion into $S^3$, then there must be a closed loop in each component of $M$'s boundary that is also Hamiltonian. This requirement is proven to be sufficient, based on a previous proof by the author and W. Zangwill.

Our analysis of 12554 cloud cases, found across four cloud clusters in space using Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer (MISR) data, revealed the presence of a distinct cloud region, which we term the "veiled core." This area, typically located in the central part of large convective clouds, is characterized by obscured features, hidden from view, behind the cloud's outer layers of forward-scattered light. Although presence of the veiled core was previously suspected, our study provides the first high-resolution visual confirmation of this area, often found in clouds with optical depths greater than 10. Leveraging MISR's capability of measuring cloud brightness from multiple perspectives, including side and rear views, we were also able to identify a second cloud region, which we call the "halo core." This area co-occurs with the veiled core and is located at multiple positions within large clouds, typically at the boundary between the cloud's dense core and its outer layers of cloud particles and adjacent clear sky. While its exact significance is still under investigation, the halo core may be a transitional area, possessing intermediate scattering properties, between the cloud's core and its surrounding parts.

By combining transparent frequencies with high absorption rates at the edges through a varying electron density, a transparent frequency range can be achieved in a directed energy system that overcomes the limitations of traditional systems. This approach enables a transparent system to operate over a vast range, significantly reducing heat generation. As a result, the transparency of the system allows for more effective integration of self-generated expansion methods, such as ion propulsion, to propel a vehicle past the point of relativistic resistance. 

Furthermore, by utilizing low-mass ions like protons and capturing a broader spectrum of directed energy through a transparent frequency range, a propulsion system can be created that utilizes a combination of laser-driven transparent directed energy and ion self-generated expansion methods to provide both power and propulsion. This system has the ability to overcome the fundamental speed restrictions imposed by directed energy systems alone. 

In addition, a proposed method of ion propulsion involves using a combination of ion collection screens, mass filters, and ion acceleration screens to control and accelerate ions in a chirped manner, thus ion self-generated thrust can be effectively harnessed as a vehicle approaches relativistic speeds. 

Overall, this system paves the way for space exploration missions to distant parts of our solar system and beyond, such as colonizing Mars and other stars.

To determine whether rocky planets orbiting other stars could support life, we first need to understand how common these worlds are. We aim to study the TOI-712 system, which has sub-Jupiter planets and appears stable. TOI-712 is an early K-type star with a relatively young age of around 2.2 billion years and long-term stability indicated by consistent rotation periods. TOI-712 b and c both exhibit signs of being partially molten due to observed photometric variations. Using astrometry from Gaia DR3, we calculated the mass density of TOI-712, which suggests the planets are likely to contain substantial amounts of hydrogen or helium. TOI-712 b and c both show significant accretion, as evidenced by excess infrared in the Spitzer MIPS 24 $\mu$m band. These planets also molten cores and H/He atmospheres disqualify them as suitable candidates for further study with JWST. However, TOI-712 does offer the opportunity to observe firsthand the process of planetary accretion.

A first-principles study has been performed to examine the physical and optical properties of four different crystallographic facets (110), (101), (001), and (100) of TiO$_{2}$ rutile. To accurately simulate these systems, three types of calculations were utilized: GW, BSE, and G$_{0}$W$_{0}$+BSE. The incorporation of carbon and nitrogen into specific Ti sites was explored, and the effects on the material's properties were analyzed through G$_{0}$W$_{0}$ and BSE methods. Carbon and nitrogen were substituted for oxygen atoms in a covalent manner, and the results showed a significant decrease in the band gap upon doping. Notably, carbon doping led to spin-polarized states within the valence band, whereas nitrogen doping did not. The optical gap values obtained from G$_{0}$W$_{0}$+BSE were in good agreement with the results from advanced many-body methods and experimental values. Carbon and nitrogen doping shifted the optical gaps to higher energies in comparison to undoped TiO$_{2}$ rutile. This letter presents a new method for producing top-quark pairs, known as "elastic production," where individual protons in colliding beams emit a virtual particle that interacts with the opposite beam's elastic proton. The mechanism we describe can facilitate the creation of top quarks alongside both forward protons. Our analysis indicates that this process, with one or no additional gluons radiated, could contribute significantly to the total cross section, possibly making up as much as 20% of the total, and thus should be taken into account in future experiments to determine how top quarks are created. We based our calculations on a specific model for the virtual particle emission known as the Eliou effect. The findings presented here may become relevant for creating rare particles like leptoquarks or slepton pairs in upcoming experiments.

To understand the complexity of the intra-cluster atmosphere, researchers utilize data-informed measurement methods to assess statistical patterns. Specifically, we examine how inaccuracies in measuring data points impact the calculation of delay vectors and subsequent cluster reconstruction, which directly relates to the complexity metric. We analyze this effect through experiments and theoretical formulas in the context of time series data characterized by distinct dynamics. Our analysis reveals that there is an optimal range for measuring delay vectors to accurately reflect the data's latency distribution, and deviations from this optimal range can lead to errors that vary linearly with the square root of the measurement deviation. This has implications for the reliability of complexity metrics, including entropy and gravitational potential, when used to evaluate the intra-cluster atmosphere's complexity. We emphasize the need to carefully assess the data's limitations to accurately interpret complexity calculations and propose further investigation to refine these assessments.

Top density $\rho$ of an infinite graph $G$ is defined as the highest density among its infinite subgraphs, and this concept is central to understanding Ramseyleft theorem for edge-colored complete infinite graphs $K_\mathbb{N}$. Although a general formula for $\rho$ was established prior, its derivation involved assuming an unknown set of possible integer values, $A$, that represent possible one-colored infinite complete subgraphs within any two-colored $K_\mathbb{N}$, and using this, it was shown that $\rho$ is directly related to the size of the smallest element in $A$. Furthermore, we provide a method to determine the exact values of $\rho$ based on specific characteristics of $A$, and illustrate this with multiple examples. Additionally, our approach to reaching these conclusions utilizes a novel technique for analyzing edge-monochromatic paths of specific lengths.

At the heart of the Galactic Central Molecular Zone, a dense cluster of stars known as the Central Molecular Zone, lies the 30.0 degrees longitude region. Within this zone, stars and gas are moving at unusually high velocities, a phenomenon often compared to a massive cosmic shaking floor. Using a novel metric called the 2D correlation length, calculated through the variance in spatial displacement of neighboring masses, researchers have discovered significant variations in the structural arrangement of gas and stars in this region. A notable negative correlation was found in the 68.0 degrees longitude direction for both H_2 and gas components detected via CO spectra data. Notably, this correlation is shorter in width among stars than in gas. Conversely, a strong positive correlation of around 0.3 parsecs is found in both directions for both gas and stars, with the positive correlation being longer among gas than in stars, a 0.5 parsecs difference in the 58.0 degrees longitude direction for both components. These 0.2 parsecs variations may be attributed to a 0.15 parsecs uncertainty found in the data. The strongest positive correlation of around 0.5 parsecs is also supported by a study using near-infrared spectroscopic data, whereas the strongest negative correlation is smaller in width, around 0.34 parsecs, likely due to a 0.13 parsecs uncertainty.
