A person-centered approach must be taken to detect and classify medical conditions,
especially when analyzing video footage. This study is the first to apply a
person-centered method using Deep Learning to detect Bell's Palsy in video clips.
We evaluate and compare different person-centered and non-person-centered
eye-classification strategies in both frame and video settings. Person-centered
classifiers were found to be more effective, with our novel NCEB video classifier
achieving superior results compared to existing methods. Moreover, our experiments
revealed that certain types of aggregations, such as maximum, minimum, or weighted
average, did not always lead to the best outcomes. Our findings indicate that
cecevid (Maximum + eye-centered) and ncevid (eye-centered) outperformed their
alternatives, with NCEB video sensitivity and specificity both exceeding 0.9.

In our community-driven quantum software platform, we've implemented the 3-D, charge-conserving sQED lattice model, adapted for qutrit-based qubits. Our tests demonstrate sub-linear scaling times and memory requirements as a function of system dimensions, enabling efficient simulation on current devices. Our code delivers optimized runtime and scalability through the use of custom data structures, achieving significant speed improvements over established quantum libraries by factors of up to 100 in some cases.

A new technique for producing high-flux streams of polarized positrons is outlined, based on using intense laser interactions with metallic surfaces to generate "jet-like" flows of both electrons and positrons. These streams can then be transformed into thicker, more manageable quantities of polarized positrons through a process called magnetic compression. By increasing the thickness of the resulting positronium, a new regime for creating positronium will be accessible, opening up new research opportunities. Additionally, a necessary condition for this regimem to be met is the development of integrated systems capable of slowing down and stopping the positrons upon interaction with an annihilation-certain target, such as implanted diamonds or similar materials doped with boron. A theoretical framework outlining this process is also outlined, along with a suggestion to experimentally verify it.

A group G is considered a limited group if its elements can be represented as logical relationships between n variables, using an element from a base set A. These logical relationships are defined by a specific type of formula that uses binary or higher-arity connections. If A consists of the numbers 0 and 1, it's equivalent to a specific type of algebraic structure known as a finite Boolean algebra. Our main achievement is demonstrating that a significant proportion - specifically, at least the square root of n times a constant - of all possible groups that can be described using these logical relationships with binary connections, are equivalent to limited groups. This demonstration utilizes the framework of the Isomorphism Leningrad Algorithm (ELI) to make comparisons.

A subthreshold CMOS-based temperature sensor circuit was developed to broaden the application of ultra-low power systems.  This subthreshold design leverages the precise voltage drop across a differential pair of transistors in subthreshold bias to perform temperature sensing.  Notably, it is capable of precise temperature sensing at extremely low supply voltages.  A 5T subthreshold sigma-delta modulator was integrated to convert the temperature signal and convert the operating range to a wider digital output.  An on-chip voltage reference generates the digital transformation clock without a separate supply, conserving area and power.  A standard 0.18$\mu$m CMOS process was used to manufacture the temperature detector, with a total chip area of just 0.11$\times$0.11 mm$^2$.  Measurements demonstrate that it operates over a supply voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V, with an average precision of 0.24$^{\circ}$C, $\pm$1.4$^{\circ}$C error over temperature, and transformation energy of 1.06nJ in a 0.3V to 3.0V output range.

Recent observations of some stars have revealed the presence of incredibly powerful magnetic fields that are concentrated into regions and maintain their intensity over time. To understand this phenomenon, we developed a theoretical model of magnetic fields that are symmetric around the star's axis in a fluid interior surrounded by the convective zone. Our analysis revealed that this class of magnetic fields is stable against perturbations breaking its axial symmetry in both the radiative and convective regions of the star's interior. We also explored the effects of the Coriolis force on magnetic fields in the convective zone and found that it contributes to the maintenance of these powerful fields by reducing turbulent decay through the $\alpha$-effect. This process is analogous to how the axial extension of the magnetic field lines by the shear at the boundary of the convective zone aids in sustaining these fields. Furthermore, we found that magnetic fields with a greater overall twist are more likely to stay stable.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) serves as a versatile non-perturbative tool in quantum field theory that can yield both conceptual insights and precise numerical results for model equations. From the one-loop level, flow equations produce simplified closed sets of flow equations for effective average actions, originating from the renormalization group's balance between the impact of newly accessible states and the modification of their phase space due to the introduced regulator. At a higher level, the framework bridges field-theoretic dynamics and optimization principles, similar to the variational renormalization group, by connecting the decrease of Hilbert space uncertainty with the effective Hamiltonian flow for imaginary time. In a simple computational setup, we suggest that closed FRG flow equations can be solved for critical points by applying the flow to transform initial guessed states into a universal state, rather than relying on flow equations' equivalence to the original model. This concept is tested for the $O(N)$ model in $d=3$ dimensions, demonstrating the flow equations' $N$-expansion discrepancies can be minimized to achieve highly accurate results for the critical exponents' coefficients.

Musical program synthesis has long been a prosperous area for music
  technology research but existing evaluation metrics fall short in capturing
  human preference. Existing methods evaluate output based on objective
  musical properties but subjectivity and context are crucial factors in
  music quality assessment. To address this gap in evaluation, we introduce
  human-centered evaluation through musical program generation and present
  Piper, a music contextual meta-model capable of refining music based on
  human-prioritized parameters. Contextual elements include but are not
  limited to tempo, key, instrumentation, and musical genre. To demonstrate
  the versatility of Piper, we applied it to the task of jazz context
  evaluation on existing musical programs. Experimental results indicate that
  the music produced by Piper aligns closely with that of top-quality
  evaluations.

This work builds key concepts from smooth geometry on Lie groupoids and stacks,
including tangent bundles, vector fields, differential forms, connections, and principal bundles.
Our approach maintains the underlying Lie groupoid structure throughout,
and relies primarily on the secondary literature, with a self-contained review,
of results from Labourie and Bcastel regarding configured principal bundles,
and incorporates the work of Alekseev and Tomasig, and Schreiber and Steiner,
into the framework of configured principal bundles over Lie groupoids and stacks.
We provide the necessary background for Schreiber and Steiner's description,
of the dB field equation solutions, of magnetic connections, and of charged particles,
in terms of configured principal bundles over Lie groupoids and stacks.

A new observation from the SubMillimeter Array reveals an unusual phenomenon: the core of the dragon infrared dark nebula, a massive star formation region, is expanding at an average rate of 1.4 cm/year. This expansion is linked to an outward pressure caused by a series of bright stars that have emerged within the region in the past 310000 years. These stars have a combined mass rate equivalent to 5.2 times 10^-6 solar masses per year. Notably, there are areas of intense activity near the region's boundaries and a newly formed binary system in its center. By comparing this to other closed molecular clouds worldwide, we see a similar pattern of central expansion prior to the onset of star formation. This phenomenon is thought to be linked to a process called inside-out collapse, which may be a critical core expansion mechanism for star formation.

Godel modal logic extends classical modal reasoning by incorporating a relational structure to predicates within each possible world. This type of logic has a correspondingly complex algebraic and relational framework that goes beyond standard algebraic and relational modal systems. Notably, Godel modal algebras can be effectively described by a local presentation based on a relational structure, which in turn generates their associated functors. Similarly, their relational frameworks are directly derived from those of their ground types. Furthermore, various extensions of Godel modal algebras can also be presented relationally.

LiDAR, or Light Detection and Ranging, uses laser technology to generate 3D point clouds for the safe and efficient design of systems, particularly in the automotive industry. However, testing this stage-by-stage process with real-world data can be both costly and time-consuming. To make prototype validation with LiDAR point clouds less cumbersome, we propose a novel approach for processing 2D and 3D point clouds that mirrors human perception and cognitive processing. Our method, Machine Intelligence for LiDAR point clouds (MILIP), breaks down LiDAR data into 5 layers and applies corresponding processes to transform raw points into a detailed environmental picture. By doing so, MILIP enables for rapid and efficient prototype testing with LiDAR point clouds. The method'sPiLAR architecture was demonstrated through a successful experiment in a dynamic scenario involving relative motion, your whose step-by-step point cloud processing led to accurate object detection and classification, your which the design can also be easily integrated with existing LiDAR processing systems.

Building on previous research, we derive explicit formulas connecting advanced and basic spectrum components of two unrelated random fields, defined on the sphere, that are stationary. These formulas apply to any level of the Gaussian spectrum and reveal a crucial distinction between two types of stationarity: one where the advanced and basic components are interconnected, and another where they are independent, characterized by an orthogonal relationship, formalized by an identity. This formulation is reminiscent of a key property of wavelets and leads to a crucial realization: a crucial condition for meeting the identity is that the basic components must possess a uniform density.

Our research analyzes the relationship between the sky locations and arrival directions of extended high-energy sources such as BL Lacertae objects and quasars in relation to neutrino arrival points recorded by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory from 2014-2018. Using Bayesian methods, we calculated the probability of random occurrences versus significant relationships, considering both maximum probable clustering and the distance between neutrino events and high-energy sources. We found no significant correlations, nor did we find any spatial clustering near sources exceeding one degree, nor near the IceCube High-Granularity Array maximum sensitivity region. These results inform future analyses and designs for high-energy source and neutrino related studies.

We investigate the flow of liquid foams through narrow tubes and discover a
corresponding pressure drop that linearly relates to the flow speed at low speeds. The
relationship is proportional to the foam's surface tension and the tube's diameter. The
proportionality factor depends on the thickness of the foam's liquid channels and
exhibits an inverse linear correlation with the Capillary Number. The thickness follows
an abrupt transition pattern in response to the Capillary Number, which we explain by
attributing the foam structure to roughness-induced hysteresis.

Skin cancer makes up to eight percent of all skin disease cases with melanoma accounting for five percent. Between one and two million people globally are affected by non-melanoma skin cancers including basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. Early detection of these cancers is crucial for effective treatment and many existing methods rely on expert opinion for diagnosis. However, getting a large number of accurate labeled images for training can be difficult, leading to the need for feature extraction techniques that reduce the dimensionality of data before classification. In this study, a new approach based on convolutional neural networks is presented which uses a new technique called Disorder to identify outlier images and remove feature extraction steps. Experimental findings show that this method accurately distinguishes between three types of skin cancers and benign moles in tests on the ISIC 2016 dataset with precisions of 99.91 percent, 99.87 percent, 99.86 percent and 99.85 percent respectively, matching or outperforming other skin diagnosis methods using the ISIC 2016 and dermnet-atl.com datasets.

As molten material is injected at room temperature, cooler boundaries cause it to cool down and solidify at a certain depth, forming a layer of liquid beneath this crust. This phenomenon is crucial in understanding the internal structure of the Earth's outer core and can also be observed in laboratory experiments studying the growth of the Earth's crust. The behavior of this two-layer system is primarily governed by the balance between viscous forces and surface tension, particularly where the different phases and boundary layers interact. The visco-elastic nature of the crust also plays a significant role in determining the system's behavior. We conducted visco-elastic Hele-Shaw cell experiments to study the growth of fingers in both Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluid systems. By adjusting the rheology of the underlying fluid and balancing the visco-elastic properties of the overhead layer, we were able to see how each factor influences the development of fingeral patterns.

This research outlines the principles of the Hamiltonian Pathway Method, a novel approach that bypasses the limitation of calculating phase space volume changes during thermal process analysis. To understand this method, we first examine the conventional approach, pointing out its shortcomings. We then detail how the method utilizes 'hyperbolic folds' to create a pathway in phase space, first applying the concept to a system expanding against a barrier, and then to a system interacting with a double-well potential, where it undergoes a swap. Our study demonstrates that by using the Hamiltonian Pathway Method, one can derive accurate results from simulated trajectories, a result that holds true for both examples and has been verified through multiple simulations. The implications of this method are broad and its theoretical underpinnings are supported by a mathematical proof of mass conservation in a control volume with moving boundaries. The significance of this research lies in its exploration of the Hamiltonian Pathway Method's role in understanding thermal and non-thermal chemical reactions. The detailed analysis of this method provides the foundation for a rigorous derivation of the Arrhenius Law, a cornerstone of reaction kinetics theory. The findings are further explored through an examination of the method's application to more complex systems and its potential to overcome the shortcomings of traditional reaction rate theories like Transition State Theory and Absolute Reaction Rate Theory. The study's outcomes are summarized with a look at its contributions to the scientific community and its potential to drive future research in the field. The analysis of this method is supported by

Spectral data from the dark molecular cloud TMC-1 revealed two distinct ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers, a challenging task due to their similar structures. Using distinct line fits, researchers identified the abundance of each isomer in the cloud. The less stable 2 position ethynyl isomer was found in smaller quantities compared to the more stable 5 position isomer. The study also explored other hydrocarbon cycle molecules and their corresponding ethynyl and nitrogen-containing counterparts. All were present in low abundances, typically between 10^-11 and 10^-14 times the abundance of H2. The findings from this study provide a foundation for laboratory spectroscopy and theoretical calculations to better understand these molecules in the interstellar medium. Furthermore, they contribute to a broader context of strange hydrocarbon molecules detected in cosmic environments including comets, meteorites, and planetary atmospheres.

When planning moves in games like Chess or Go, top-tier machines focus on anticipating the outcomes of future moves rather than just evaluating the current position. This research introduces a novel approach, Look-ahead Focus (LAF), for generating features in machine interpretation that looks several moves ahead. LAF adapts the concept of selective attention from the field of machine learning by applying it to the CINDA-2.0 interpretation model. The method is simplified, incorporating a streamlined architecture and a basic formulation of the look-ahead mechanism. The results show that the method significantly outperforms the existing CINDA-2.0 model in both speed and accuracy while maintaining comparable performance to the best-in-class methods. The LAF method's the parameter's effect was also analyzed through experimentation.

Computer scientists have long used the translational method to tackle complex design challenges. This approach involves breaking down a problem into smaller, manageable parts that can be individually solved and then integrated. Notably, Carl Hewitt utilized this method to create the FLO-2 translational compiler, a significant milestone in grid computing history. His work demonstrated how grid computing can be achieved by dividing a problem into smaller components, solving them individually, and combining the solutions. This translational approach has far-reaching implications for computer system design and has consistently been applied to create more efficient systems throughout computer science development.

A new form of fluid has been discovered whose characteristics align with those of matter-like dark energy, potentially facilitating the resolution of several persistent challenges in cosmology, including the cosmological constant problem, the coincidence problem, and the nature of matter and dark matter in the early universe. In this study, the impact of dissipation on the fluid's evolution was examined within the framework of general relativity, in both a static and rotating universe, and how dissipation affects the stability of this fluid was investigated, leading to the development and testing of a dynamic model based on field equations, resulting in the conclusion that a significant aspect of this model's trajectories was made possible due to the presence of friction forces in a static universe, until the formation of big bang singularity, and finally, the outcome that matter and dark matter would become dark matter-like due to dissipation during the early universe.

In contemporary society, fostering life-long learning and a positive attitude towards knowledge is crucial for effective societal development, and curiosity has been recognized as a vital engine for lifelong learning. Numerous prior studies have explored various aspects of curiosity, yet they lack an in-depth understanding of how curiosity changes dynamically during learning and the influence of social interaction on its development. To address these knowledge gaps, we introduce a pioneering approach that utilizes eye-tracking and sentiment analysis in conjunction with Hidden Markov Models to examine the complex relationship between brain activity, emotional state, and learning behavior in a real-world small group learning setting. Our findings reveal distinct patterns in eye movement and sentiment that differentiate individuals driven by curiosity from those motivated by extraneous factors, and also demonstrate that curious learners are more likely to engage in content-related social interaction and contribute valuable information that informs their peers. Notably, our model outperforms existing benchmarks in accurately predicting curiosity and demonstrating enhanced generalizability.

Recent advances in graph neural networks have primarily relied on graph convolutional operators, whose design has limited innovation. A new approach is now being explored, re-framing graph-structured data through positive definite functions, which can be used to construct a covariance matrix. This approach has the potential to incorporate various features, including Mat\'ern functions in Euclidean space. By formulating graph data with a posdef kernel that combines Mat\'ern functions in Euclidean space and the graph adjacency matrix, the new approach retains the matting effect of Mat\'ern functions while enabling information propagation across nodes via the graph adjacency matrix. Analytical results now prove the redundancy of positive definite functions in theory, yet highlight the performance benefits of mixing functions in both Euclidean space and graph topology. By conducting experiments on both real-world and fabricated datasets, the new approach has demonstrated improved classification results compared to existing graph neural network models.

The effectiveness of planning and managing a city's road network relies on accurate data, a scalable performance measure for urban road networks is proposed. This observation network design aims to accurately observe the speed of the city's traffic while minimizing the number of detectors used. Initially, a discrete optimization approach was tested on a real-world dataset of the New York City road system, but due to the large size of the dataset, a gradient-based method was developed for faster results. The proposed observation network demonstrated an efficient scale of detection as the number of proposed detectors increased linearly with the road network size, achieving a speed estimation performance comparable to the benchmark method on the NYC road system.

By incorporating the $J/\psi\to (\gamma + ){\rm invisible}$ process into our analysis, we find that the current bounds on the neutrino mass and the micro-black hole (MBH) mass are significantly improved, particularly in case (2). The new constraints on neutrino mass and MBH mass are also equal, yielding $2.3\times 10^{-6}$ eV, which aligns with cosmological predictions for the effective number of neutrino species and the Planck Planck mass. Consequently, two valid solutions for the effective number of neutrino species and the Planck Planck mass emerge, each corresponding to different values of the form factor for the MBH decay process, namely $0.015$ and $0.045$ for the respective solutions.

Traditional methods for solving initial value problems involve advancing the solution from one time step to the next using a fixed or adaptive time step. In contrast, simultaneous difference and variation methods solve the entire time interval at once by approximating both the solution and time within a problem-specific subspace. Though SDIMSIMs have been successfully applied to boundary value problems and turn-back problems, their application to initial value problems is hindered by their requirement to solve a large nonlinear algebraic system, which becomes computationally expensive over an extensive time interval. To address this, we propose modifying typical SDIMSIMs by solving the algebraic system only at the beginning and intermediate times, then updating the solution and time independently during each small sub-interval. This approach leverages the mature concepts of fixed or adaptive time stepping, enabling more efficient computational resources. Numerical experiments demonstrate significant improvements in computational times while maintaining high solution accuracy.

Functional singular spectrum analysis is a recent innovation that assesses and evaluates time-varying, high-dimensional data sets containing multiple variables and extensive datasets. Its effectiveness has been tested with synthetic datasets and an examination of U.S. Treasury Yield curves. Its capabilities have been demonstrated with real data sets such as German Economic Statistics and U.S. Macroeconomic Time Series.

Autoevals, or self-generated testing frameworks, are commonly used in the process of creating advanced systems to ensure they are free from harmful outputs. Although there is a common misconception that the effectiveness of these frameworks is a matter of technical improvement, the evaluation of their reliability is, in reality, a crucial management issue. The stability of both autoevals in their current state and their scalability in the future are, in reality, severely hampered, leading to the risk of leaking training information and struggling to generalize to novel, unseen cases. It appears that autoevals are both unduly sensitive to minor variations and excessively biased, as they are, in reality, designed to be met with ease by optimal models through overfitting and prone to quickly incorporate the performance boost from co-tuning due to the emergence of narrow criteria that are difficult to satisfy, leaving little room for the kind of margin required to ensure the validity of the value judgments being made. Undeniably, the choice of scoring rules, the design of prompt prompts and the selection of candidate outputs are all crucial factors that need to be carefully managed to ensure the reliability of the value judgments being made.

In the context of random walks in one dimension, we investigate the relationship between local and global properties of an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process subject to an indicator force, modeled by the stochastic differential equation with a Heaviside function. The study focuses on the persistence of time spent on one side of the state space and how it relates to the time it takes for the process to reach its first zero point, starting from a positive initial value. By analyzing both theoretical models and numerical simulations, an approximate formula for local duration is derived and validated through exact computations of key parameters, confirming the relationship between local and global quantities of interest. Additionally, a similar result for a process without the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck damping term is also obtained. Overall, this work emphasizes the persistent nature of time local durations in random walks.

The IShTAR facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is an advanced test chamber designed to study plasma and has been in operation since 2017. Its 11 meter diameter allows for a variety of experiments, and its modular system includes a plasma generator that can produce different plasma modes, including the helicon mode which is used in laboratory and space plasmas. This paper outlines the design of the helicon plasma generator, and analyzes data from plasma measurements obtained during both low and high power operations. By comparing calculated and measured parameters, including density, temperature, and power transfer efficiency, we demonstrate the correct function of the helicon plasma generator. Its performance was also enhanced with the addition of a matching network, which increased power transfer efficiency to over 90 percent.

In our study, we developed a mathematical model to analyze the effectiveness of a microbial pesticide system that releases the fungus Entomopathogenic Nematode to eliminate soft scale insects, followed by applying a general pesticide to reduce the pesticide's negative impact on the target insect population. A set of equations was constructed to model this system, which was then examined for the existence and stability of specific solutions representing the coexistence of all population entities. A key measure called Lyapunov exponent was introduced to identify turning points in system behavior, where a significant shift occurs in the deterministic system's dynamics. Furthermore, we applied stochastic differential equations to account for the presence of noise in the biological system, ultimately revealing that noise has a deterministic equivalent and can influence the existence of a particular solution.

A key challenge in computational pathology is automating the detection and analysis of cancer cells in histopathology images to streamline the labor-intensive process of pathology diagnosis. While previous methods have made progress, they often struggle to accurately identify nuclei due to the complexity of the images and the high variability in nuclear appearance. To tackle this challenge, a novel two-stage network called W-Net has been developed, which effectively combines the tasks of image classification and nucleus detection. In the first stage, the network uses a fully convolutional structure to generate a rough nucleus map, which in turn guides the extraction of relevant image features through an attention mechanism. These refined features are then employed in the second stage to produce a precise nucleus map. By iterating between these two stages, the network continuously refines both the rough map and the extracted features, ultimately achieving accurate nucleus detection. Experimental evaluations on public datasets prove the effectiveness of this innovative approach.

In a specific local field scenario of characteristic greater than two, this study establishes the special orthogonal and symplectic groups' ability to uniquely identify a set of non-zero numbers up to a specific scaling factor, which is crucial for these groups. This study achieves that level of uniqueness for special orthogonal and symplectic groups over a specific class of field types.

Graph theory research has long focused on graph properties that could indicate the presence of a hamiltonian cycle in an original graph. However, for certain graphs, such as line graphs, traditional parameters may not provide accurate predictions. This paper introduces two novel parameters - the iterated line graph and the hamiltonian pathway index - which successfully detect the presence of a hamiltonian cycle in a graph and its iterated line graph. These parameters are defined based on the relationship between subgraphs of increasing complexity. While complexity-based definitions have produced successful results in previous research, they remain relatively unexplored. This paper builds on that existing work by extending the focus to include iterated line graphs.

COVID-19 infections can lead to pyroptosis, a form of cell death, resulting from the lysis of infected cells due to inflammatory processes. This cell death is triggered by the formation of GSDMD-N fragments, which can be initiated by proteases such as caspase-1, -4, -11, and the NLRP3 inflammasome. Our simple mathematical model explores how GSDMD-N fragments accumulate, leading to pyroptosis, in response to SARS-CoV-1/2 infections and the effects of doxycycline and IL-1Ra treatments. We find that the model can effectively capture the behaviors of uncontrolled pyroptosis, GSDMD-N fragment buildup during pyroptosis, and the counteracting influences of doxycycline and IL-1Ra, the latter preventing pyroptosis when administered before infection. Furthermore, an extension to this model allows for the examination of the NLRP3 inflammasome's role in responding to reactive oxygen species produced by infections, while the effects of doxycylline modelled in this extended framework can be observed through a reduction in GSDMD-N fragment levels due to the regulated NLRP3 inflammasome.

External state variables and inaccurate incentive signals can hinder reinforcement learning systems, leading to the development of inefficient or harmful behaviors. Extrinsic motivation, common in reinforcement learning applications, introduces new, possibly deceptive external states and rewards. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a framework for analyzing and tackling external state variables and incentive issues in reinforcement learning, building on established theories from economics and psychology. Our approach then proposes a novel reinforcement learning algorithm capable of discovering and remitting the removal of external state variables and incentives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by comparing it to baseline approaches in a task involving the reversal of Aviar's trap, outperforming them in terms of efficiency.

The consensus mechanism in blockchain projects relies on a software system that processes input data and generates output based on previously stored information. This paper presents a high-level specification using refinement types and an accompanying compiler for this system. By utilizing this approach, we can statically detect errors in the blockchain system before deployment, including issues with security and functionality. Building upon an existing internal language for the Tezos blockchain, HELMHOLTZ extends the system with refinement types to validate the correct implementation of Tezos smart contracts or multi-agent systems. This paper specifically focuses on Helmholtz, our refinement type language, its connection to the DCPSDC operational semantics, and its application in validating the refinement of Tezos systems.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are versatile systems that adapt traditional CNNs to operate on graph-structured data, bridging the gap between data formats. GCNNs generate feature vectors of optimized dimensionality for each node, enabling high-performance classification, clustering, and other tasks. Despite their effectiveness, the precise mechanism behind their efficiency remains unclear. In this paper, a novel match filter (MF) approach is presented to bridge the theoretical and practical applications of GCNNs. By analyzing the MF match, it is demonstrated that GCNNs emulate the systems' optimal performance by adapting traditional CNNs to graph-structured data. Furthermore, GCNNs are seen to be equivalent to optimal filter (OMF) systems that leverage node labels and neighborhood node features. Through experiments, several GCNN strategies are evaluated, highlighting their performance in various tasks and providing insights into their operational mechanisms.

Einstein's General Relativity can be described using a Chern-Simons-like action by expressing the Einstein-Cartan 1-form as the derivative of the Lorentz connection, augmented with a boundary term. In this paper, we extend this analogy to include a scalar field, employing a BPS-type extension. By utilizing the Ito-Takahashi formulation, which employs group-valued derivatives, we derive equations of motion that include a non-Abelian covariant derivative for both a solitonic configuration and a black hole solution. Specifically, we find that the gravitational dressing of a scalar field can give rise to an Hairy Black Hole when the appropriate boundary conditions are met, or remain hidden in a solitonic solution for other boundary conditions. We also establish a duality between these solutions within the same extended Chern-Simons-like action.

Theories that integrate branes equivalent to the dual of the fundamental string, such as D1/FP systems in type II theories, can exhibit the exchange of left and right-moving components. This  L/R- symmetry allows for an increase in supercharges through a process known as a BPS jump. The corresponding Lagrangian systems can be viewed as being associated with certain mathematical structures called sigma models over specific manifolds that possess a rich set of symmetries. The key feature of these manifolds is the presence of subgroups within their T-duals that permit for an involution, which is then mapped to a corresponding subgroup in the algebraic structure of the Kac–Moody Lie algebras. This allows us to derive a set of equations that relate the generators of these algebras, which in turn can be utilized in the construction of non-commutative generalizations of affine Weyl group actions. These actions can be applied to expand the algebra and introduce additional branes, such as D3-branes, into brane configurations, such as D1/D5/D3 systems.

In ultrasound elastography, determining the synthetic aperture's lateral shift accurately is crucial for generating high-resolution images. However, due to the data acquisition method used in synthetic aperture techniques, where ultrasound signals are collected sequentially at each sensor element without simultaneous transmission, there are timing discrepancies that distort range equations and hinder image reconstruction. While previous approaches corrected these errors by introducing virtual transmission and reception elements, these methods complicate image reconstruction and reduce processing efficiency. In this study, we developed an algorithm called Virtual Origin (VO) SA, which places the virtual transmission and reception elements at the array center for fractional cycle delays and then shifts them laterally for other types of delays. Because the elements are centered in the VO SA method, it is possible to use a fast and efficient reconstruction technique known as the shifted inverse synthetic aperture correlation technique (SISACR). Furthermore, theoretical and simulation results show that the VO SA method provides high precision in estimating lateral shifts and image resolution, and can also be utilized to enhance the performance of the conventional synthetic aperture technique (SACR).

Algorithms and corresponding pseudocode are frequently analyzed in computer science research and instruction. Meanwhile, demonstration-based learning in the field of machine learning also focuses on teaching agents how to execute tasks effectively. This work introduces the concept of "Rational Pseudocode," which seeks to connect these two fields. A key aspect of this concept is the introduction of the most efficient pseudocode that accurately depicts the underlying true algorithm. This optimal pseudocode can be seen as a compressed representation of the algorithm, similar to the principle of optimal code compression. The concept of rational pseudocode gives rise to several theoretically meaningful properties, including the emergence of a prior over algorithms as a result of minimizing code length. A simple gradient-based method is then proposed to approximate this ideal pseudocode. This method evaluates candidate codes based on how well they compress the observed behavioral data. The proposed framework is then applied to real-world examples, including the Shortest Path problem and a computational complexity benchmark, NC-KT. The results highlight the ability of rational pseudocode to produce clear and concise code for algorithms with efficient compressed states. In contrast, for algorithms that are unnecessarily complex, their elaborate internal structures mirror their suboptimal efficiency.

A poset $\pi$ is considered $B_n$-ramsey if there exists a positive integer $m$ such that in any $n$-coloring of the Boolean algebra $B_m$, at least one $\pi$ appears colored a single color. The collection of $B_n$-ramsey posets form the subject of growing research within combinatorial theory. This paper extends that research by analyzing $B_n$-ramsey posets that are located in the Boolean algebra as $V$-shaped subsets, resulting in several new results and an exploration of potential generalizations.

In response to the persistent challenge of organizing massive amounts of multimedia and text data, supervised methods like classification have long been effective, but require significant initial effort to classify new incoming data. Unsupervised clustering offers a viable alternative, eliminates the need for prior labeling, and enables discovery of novel patterns, but typically lacks the ability to handle new data dynamically. In this research, we present an efficient unsupervised algorithm that progressively group similar data and adapts to new information in real-time, utilizing new techniques to minimize computational costs as it processes a series of inputs by numerical vectors. Our method effectively scales to high-dimensional spaces and vehicle- video reflow scenarios, and when compared to state-of-the-art alternatives, it achieves optimal performance, especially with video data. For detailed results, please refer to the associated supplementary material. Our code is freely available on GitHub under a permissive license.

We investigate a class of hierarchical stochastic pursuit-flight games where the rate of change in size is influenced by a factor inversely proportional to the product of the two populations. This model is suitable for analyzing both biological phenomena, such as bacterial phage interactions, and economic scenarios, like the relationship between company stocks and market liquidity. A key finding is the existence of a stable state, or orbit, consisting of multiple nested, discrete population divisions that maintain their relative structures. The equilibrium rate of change in this multi-layered environment is at least as high as the sum of the equilibrium rates of the separate, individual divisions. Additionally, we examine the stability of orbit in response to sudden changes in the environment.

You're likely familiar with the concept of circular preferences, which we discuss in the context of likelihoods. A nontransitive probability measure occurs when the fact that A is more likely than B, and B is more likely than C, does not guarantee the same relationship between A and C. We investigate the conditions under which the relationship between A and C may be different, potentially reversing the expected nontransitive outcome. Our analysis utilizes a model based on the relative positions of points to establish the exact conditions for both circular and nontransitive likelihoods, and we provide methods to implement these conditions, as well as a way to model the resulting "surprises" that arise from these relationships.

Recently, deep learning techniques have significantly lowered the doses used in computed tomography (CT) scanning while maintaining image quality, with noise reduction models playing a key role in achieving this quality with lower doses. However, these models struggle to balance quality and dose reduction, and using them across various low-dose scans can lead to poor image artifacts and dose control issues due to their fixed training and generalization limitations. To address these problems, a new cycle-consistent, switchable network has been developed for low-dose CT denoising. This network adapts its generation style based on input data to minimize artifacts and ensures the dose-range invariance of the denoised images, thus providing the ability to effectively reduce noise in low-dose CT scans without needing to fine-tune the model. Although cycle-consistent switchable networks exist, their application to medical imaging is limited due to their difficulty in achieving global optimization. To overcome this, the proposed network adds an auxiliary loss term, allowing it to be optimized more easily and applied to various clinical computed tomography (CT) scenarios. The model's performance has been validated on multiple low-dose cancer and cardiac CT datasets, showing its ability to reduce noise effectively and efficiently.

Recent advances in dialog understanding have been heavily reliant on pre-training with extensive supervised data, however, this approach faces limitations due to the scarcity of annotated multi-turn dialog datasets. To overcome this challenge, our work introduces SPACE-2, a novel tree-structured contrastive pre-training framework that makes use of unsupervised data while incorporating available annotated turns as contrastive examples. In this model, the dialog state is constructed from the hierarchical relationships between utterances learned through unsupervised pre-training, and contrasting the hidden states of child utterances with those of parent nodes as well as annotated turns helps the model grasp the global context within each dialog. Our experiments show that SPACE-2 achieves superior performance compared to baseline models, yielding notable improvements in overall dialog understanding and related metrics.

Considering a conformal Ricci-Yamabe transformation, a potential function $\mathcal{f}$, and a constant $\mathcal{y}$, we examine the ideal fluid spacetime to determine whether its metric is conformal to the scalar curvature when associated with a conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton. In this context, the vector field $\xi$ represents the gradient of the potential function $\mathcal{f}$ multiplied by a scalar $l$, where $|\mathcal{y}| \neq 0$ and $\mathcal{y}$ is orthogonal to $\xi$. By analyzing the geometric properties of the vector field $\xi$, we establish that it can be a conformal Killing vector field, a null eigenvector of the Ricci tensor, or the metric of the spacetime can be $\kappa$-Einstein metric. Additionally, we examine whether a conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton can be expanding, steady, or shrinking based on the constant $\mathcal{y}$.

Research on spinning, distorted halo nuclei is predicted to reveal a form of decoupling where the core's spin properties are separated from those of the nuclear skin. Utilizing a four-nucleon decoupled-ABCD model, we are capable of simulating a rotating, distorted core in conjunction with the skin, and have found that the spin decoupling is robust. It has also been found that, in terms of decoupling, certain properties such as the core's spin and decoupling effects are only mildly impacted by factors such as the mass of the skin nucleons, as well as both spin and decoupling are exhibited strong sensitivity to the parameterization of the mean field, particularly in terms of a critical parameter known as $\beta_1$, which characterizes the shape of the skin.

In the field of video super-resolution, the GT-mime model has been widely adopted in recent years. Furthermore, despite significant advances in image super-resolution, video super-resolution lags behind due to additional difficulties stemming from temporal variations and the requirement of preserving consistency. To overcome these challenges, we introduce an improved version of the BasicVSR architecture, specifically BasicVSR++, which comprises two key enhancements: introducing guided attention networks to effectively capture temporal information, and replacing the conventional alignment module with cross-enhanced transmission (CET) that leverages guidance from both the low-resolution and high-resolution videos. Through comprehensive objective and user studies, we demonstrate that BasicVSR++ outperforms not only its predecessor, but also state-of-the-art video super-resolution models.

Precision predictions for particle physics theories necessanary to interpret experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) rely heavily on accurately modeling weak bosons radiated during parton interactions in proton collisions. While weak bosons can be identified via their decay products, another method involves using forward detectors like ALICE-TOF and LHCb to detect the weak bosons themselves. This method, though powerful, is complicated due to the significant momentum carried by these weak bosons, often hidden within the total transverse momentum of the produced particles. To overcome this challenge, researchers used machine learning to create an algorithm capable of efficiently separating weak bosons from other radiated particles using the data collected by the ALICE and LHC detectors. This algorithm achieved exceptional performance, with values of 0.89 and 0.97 for precision vector boson fraction estimation with the ALICE and LHC configurations respectively. By leveraging additional information from the hit pattern of the ALICE detector, additional research found that this weak boson identification efficiency could be increased, resulting in a 0.12 value of $\kappa$, determined by muon multiplicity.

Our investigation focuses on the influence of model-based reinforcement learning in a model-driven learning framework as a mechanism to anticipate and manage unexpected events. We further examine its potential to support a form of implicit, catastrophic failure avoidance in a model-driven multi-task reinforcement learning framework. To address the challenges associated with this focus, we designed and executed a series of simulated experiments set within a controlled, multi-task reinforcement learning environment, featuring deliberate, sudden, and sudden events. To investigate the general applicability of our approach, we created a simplified, abstract model. Our research reveals that, in response to sudden, catastrophic events, agents can implicitly develop a form of protective behavior, akin to that seen in some animal species, without any explicit reward for such actions. Moreover, our approach allows the agents to continue engaging with the environment, gathering information, and acquiring new skills. To demonstrate the utility of our approach in a more complex setting, we developed a simple, abstract model and conducted additional experiments. We also explored the role of model decoupling in allowing agents to anticipate and avoid sudden, catastrophic events.

A new class of nonlinear partial differential equations, comprising the porous medium kind equations and the swift diffusion kind equations, is examined on a complete, non-compact metric measure space that has a compact boundary. The equation's coefficients are allowed to vary with both the spatial location and the time. Under the condition that the underlying space satisfies a specific curvature bound and contains no positive time-dependent curvature, we derive an explicit, uniform estimate for the rate at which the solution decreases over time. This estimation improves upon previous work by Remmen and the author, providing a more precise bound within the same context of non-compact metric measure spaces with a compact boundary.

We explore the Godel-Carnap Theorem, a comprehensive theory of recursion that generalizes original results by Godel and Tarski on unprovability and the lack of a total ordering operator, as well as their joint finding on the unprovability of consistency. In this context, we also consider the role of Rosser's improvement of Godel's First Theorem. Our main achievement is a detailed investigation of the aspects of strength, totality, and monotonicity of specific functions, which leads to a generalized result with additional insights. This generalization extends A. Kechris's work on the unprovability of set-theoretic well-orderedness in arithmetic systems. We provide a total proof of our generalized result. Given its nature, we believe this result may have further extensions, and we discuss the associated open questions.

In Clifford analysis, non-zero functions that satisfy certain differential equations can be decomposed into components characterized by integer parts, similar to writing integers as a sum of digits. Given a compact domain in R^n, this research explores conditions under which a function, defined by certain differential properties and values at its boundary, can be fully represented as the sum of its components. A key application of these conditions is their potential use in eigenfunctions of the Laplace operator on a given domain.

The standard Consecutive k-arrangement Response (CKR) sampling technique has long been utilized in the design of statistical surveys. Its versatility has also facilitated the development of various other survey sampling methods, including those based on systematic and circular arrangements. The objective of this research is to provide a revised version of the Consecutive k-arrangement method that maintains the same level of precision as the original, while offering greater ease of execution and enhanced stability in the associated variance. The original Consecutive k-arrangement method was first introduced by Yates in 1960. Its underlying principle involved selecting a random starting point and then choosing subsequent units based on an interval of k. The new technique, which we call Modified Consecutive k-arrangement (MCR) sampling, uses a different approach by dividing the population into non-overlapping clusters and randomly choosing one cluster from each of k consecutive divisions. A key advantage of the MCR sampling method is that it greatly reduces the intricate computations required for variance estimation, and also offers greater ease of execution and better stability in the associated variance. A simulation study was conducted to evaluate and compare the variance estimation techniques, and the outcomes of this study show that the MCR sampling method can provide more precise variance estimates than both the Consecutive k-arrangement (CR) sampling and the simple random (SRS) sampling techniques.
